prompt: Priya calls at 11:40 a.m. and asks to buy open-end fund shares at the NAV printed on the statement she read at breakfast. The purchase is priced:

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the last published quote with the purchase price. A call before the close does not lock the statement NAV; the order waits for the next computed NAV.

distractorExplanations.d: Pushes a late-morning order to the following business day. An order received before the day's pricing time gets that day's NAV, still uncomputed at 11:40 a.m.

Absent on Class A, because that class collects its sales cost through the annual marketing fee
A front-end sales charge deducted from her money on the day she buys the Class A shares

explanation: Class A shares carry a front-end sales charge, deducted from the amount invested at purchase. That one-time sales charge is not a level 12b-1 fee. A 12b-1 fee is an ongoing fund expense and can exist beside the front-end load; it does not replace it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the front-end sales charge with a level 12b-1 fee. The 12b-1 fee is an annual fund expense, not the charge taken off Helen's purchase.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns Class B's contingent deferred sales charge to Class A. Class A is the front-end class, not the declining back-end class.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops the front-end charge and leaves only a marketing fee. Class A is defined by the sales charge at purchase, which is separate from any 12b-1 fee.

prompt: Luis is offered Class B shares and asks what comes off his money on the day he buys. Those shares typically:

options.text: Carry a declining contingent deferred sales charge on an early redemption, not a front-end load at purchase
Take a front-end sales charge out of the purchase on day one, the same structure Class A uses on the ticket
Add a separate commission on top of NAV at the ticket and then drop every sales charge if he leaves early
Carry no sales charge of either kind, because a missing front-end load means the class is no-load from the start

explanation: Class B shares typically have no front-end load. The sales charge is a contingent deferred sales charge that declines the longer the shares are held and is paid if the client redeems early. Buying at NAV on day one does not make the class no-load.

distractorExplanations.b: Copies the Class A front-end load onto Class B. Class B typically does not deduct a sales charge from the purchase on day one.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a commission stacked on NAV at purchase and then waives the exit charge. The Class B charge is the declining contingent deferred sales charge, paid if he leaves early.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the lack of a front-end load as a no-load class. Class B still carries a contingent deferred sales charge that declines over the holding period.

prompt: Sam expects to hold an open-end fund for a very long time and likes Class C shares because today's ticket shows no large upfront charge. Class C shares:

options.text: Match Class A on a long hold, so the small ticket means he already received the front-end breakpoint
Are the level-load class, so a higher 12b-1 fee keeps running through the years of that very long hold

That level charge makes Class C a poor default for a very long holding chosen only because today's ticket is small. A short contingent deferred sales charge, common on Class C, is not the end of the load.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats Class C as if it were Class A with a breakpoint already applied. Class C does not use the front-end breakpoint schedule.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the end of a short contingent deferred sales charge with the end of the load. The level 12b-1 fee continues, so the small ticket is not the whole cost of a very long hold.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns Class A's front-end load to Class C. Class C is chosen in part because the purchase ticket does not carry that upfront charge.

prompt: Wei asks for the public offering price of an open-end fund. NAV is 19.20 and the sales charge is 4 percent. That offering price is:

options.text: 18.43, which rounds the result of multiplying 19.20 by 0.96
19.97, which rounds the result of multiplying 19.20 by 1.04
20.00, which is 19.20 divided by one minus the 4 percent charge
19.24, which adds four cents to the 19.20 NAV and treats 4 percent as four cents

explanation: The public offering price equals NAV divided by one minus the sales charge. The sales charge is a percent of the offering price, not a percent added on top of NAV. Here that is 19.20 / (1 − 0.04) = 19.20 / 0.96 = 20.00. Multiplying by 1.04, multiplying by 0.96, or adding 0.04 uses the wrong base.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies NAV by 0.96, which subtracts 4 percent from NAV. The offering price is NAV divided by 0.96, not NAV times 0.96.
distractorExplanations.b: Multiplies NAV by 1.04, as if the sales charge were added on top of NAV. The charge comes out of the offering price, so the divisor is 0.96.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds 0.04 to NAV and treats 4 percent as four cents. A 4 percent sales charge is not a four-cent add-on to 19.20.

prompt: Gina signs a letter of intent so purchases she still plans to make can count toward a breakpoint in the same fund family. The letter is:

options.text: A promise that the fund's NAV will stand higher when the letter's term ends
The representative's guarantee that this fund will beat the other funds in its category
A lock on today's NAV, so each later purchase in the family fills at the price on the day she signs
Her intent to add later purchases in the family, which lets her take the lower sales charge now

explanation: A letter of intent lets the client qualify now for a breakpoint by counting purchases she intends to make later in the same fund family. The usual term is 13 months. It says nothing about how the fund will perform. If she does not complete the intended purchases, the fund can collect the higher sales charge that would have applied.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the letter into a performance promise. A letter of intent reduces the sales charge; it does not promise that NAV will stand higher.
distractorExplanations.b: Makes the representative guarantee relative performance. The letter does not promise that the fund will beat its category.
distractorExplanations.c: Freezes the purchase price. Later purchases are still priced under forward pricing; the letter only helps the sales-charge breakpoint.

prompt: Devon already holds shares in one fund family and is adding a new purchase in that family. Rights of accumulation let the new purchase:

options.text: Count the shares already held in that family toward the sales-charge breakpoint on this new purchase
Combine with a holding at an unrelated fund family so the two sponsors share one lower sales charge
Skip the sales charge, because the shares he already owns were charged on the day he first bought them
Freeze the return on the old shares, so the new purchase cannot change the outcome of what he already holds

explanation: Rights of accumulation count holdings the client already has in the same fund family toward the breakpoint on a new purchase. The breakpoint is a lower sales charge at a larger amount in that family. Holdings at an unrelated sponsor are not included, and the right does not wipe out the sales charge or lock in a return.

distractorExplanations.b: Pools an unrelated fund family into the breakpoint. Rights of accumulation stay inside the same family; a second sponsor's shares do not count.
distractorExplanations.c: Waives the sales charge because older shares were already charged. Accumulation can lower the charge on the new purchase; it does not erase it.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the right as a performance lock. Rights of accumulation affect the sales-charge breakpoint, not the return on shares he already holds.

prompt: Aisha sees a 12b-1 fee on an open-end fund's fee table and asks whether she pays it once, as a check at the purchase. The 12b-1 fee is:

options.text: The same one-time front-end load Class A shares deduct from a purchase, listed under a marketing name
An ongoing expense drawn from fund assets over time, not a one-time front-end load at the ticket
A dollar commission the representative adds on top of NAV at purchase and does not assess again
A yearly cash rebate the fund pays her to return the sales charge she paid at purchase

explanation: A 12b-1 fee is an ongoing expense of the fund, used for distribution and shareholder service and taken from fund assets over time. It is part of what the expense ratio reflects. It is not a one-time front-end sales charge the client pays at the ticket, and it is not a rebate of that charge.

distractorExplanations.a: Renames the front-end load as a 12b-1 fee. The front-end load is deducted at purchase; the 12b-1 fee continues as a fund expense.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the fee into a one-time commission stacked on NAV. A 12b-1 fee is assessed as an ongoing fund expense, not as an add-on the representative writes on the ticket once.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the direction of the fee. The 12b-1 fee is paid out of fund assets; the fund does not rebate it to Aisha as cash.

prompt: Andre exchanges shares of one open-end fund for shares of another fund in the same family. He asks if the move is tax-free and free of a new front-end load. The exchange is generally:

options.text: Tax-free on its own, because a switch that stays inside the family does not sell the old shares
Charged a new front-end load, as if he were buying the second fund for the first time at the public offering price
Executed at NAV without a new front-end load, and it is not tax-free by itself in a taxable account
Treated as a Section 1035 exchange, so the gain waits the way an annuity-to-annuity transfer would

explanation: An exchange inside the same fund family is generally made at NAV and does not add a new front-end sales charge. The exchange privilege does not, by itself, make the move tax-free. In a taxable account the switch is a redemption and a new purchase, so it can realize a gain or a loss.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the family exchange as tax-free. Staying in the family prices the trade at NAV; it does not stop the exchange from being a taxable sale in a taxable account.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds a new front-end load. A same-family exchange is generally executed at NAV, not at the public offering price of a first-time purchase.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the fund exchange with a Section 1035 annuity exchange. A same-family fund switch is not a 1035 transfer, and it is not tax-free by itself.

prompt: At 1:15 p.m. Camille asks her representative to redeem open-end fund shares and to lock the price then showing on the screen. That redemption is priced:

options.text: At the screen price, which the representative may lock for a redemption placed before the close
At yesterday's NAV, which stays the redemption price until the fund prices again the next morning
At a price the representative negotiates with another shareholder who wants to buy the shares she is leaving
At the next computed NAV after the order is received, which the representative cannot lock at 1:15 p.m.

explanation: An open-end redemption uses forward pricing. The shares are redeemed at the next NAV computed after the fund receives the order. The figure on the screen at 1:15 p.m. is not a price the representative can lock. Camille's afternoon order, received before the day's pricing time, receives that day's NAV once it is computed.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets the representative lock the mid-day screen price. Open-end redemptions are not filled at a quote frozen during the day.
distractorExplanations.b: Holds yesterday's NAV open as today's redemption price. The redemption waits for the next computed NAV, not the prior close.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the redemption into a negotiated trade with another shareholder. The fund redeems the shares; the representative does not find a buyer.

prompt: Ken wants a money-market fund because he believes each share is stuck at one dollar and the government stands behind it. The representative should explain that the fund:

options.text: Seeks a stable NAV, and that goal is not a government guarantee that each share stays at one dollar
Carries a government guarantee that each share stays at one dollar no matter what the portfolio does
Holds bank deposits, so FDIC insurance covers each shareholder the way a savings account would cover Ken
Aims to grow NAV the way a stock fund does, and the government pays Ken if the share price falls

explanation: A money-market fund seeks a stable NAV. That objective is not a government guarantee that each share stays at one dollar, and it is not FDIC insurance. The portfolio holds short-term instruments, not a savings account. If the fund cannot maintain the stable NAV, the share price can move.

distractorExplanations.b: Turns a stable-NAV objective into a government guarantee. No government promise keeps the money-market share at one dollar.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the fund with an insured bank deposit. A money-market fund is an investment company product, not an FDIC-insured savings account.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns a stock-fund objective and a government makeup payment. The fund seeks a stable NAV and does not come with a government payment if the price moves.

prompt: Jonah owns an interval fund and asks to redeem his entire position this afternoon, the way he redeems his open-end mutual fund. The interval fund:

options.text: Redeems at the next NAV every business day, on the same terms as the open-end fund he already owns
Repurchases shares on a set schedule, so he cannot cash out this afternoon the way his open-end fund does
Lists the shares on an exchange, so he can sell the whole position to another buyer at the bid this afternoon
Must be held until a stated maturity, with no repurchase available to him before that date arrives

explanation: An interval fund repurchases shares on a set schedule. It does not offer the daily redemption window of an open-end mutual fund, so Jonah cannot turn the position in this afternoon the way he redeems that fund. The shares are also not a continuous exchange listing he can sell at the bid.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the interval fund daily open-end liquidity. Repurchases happen on the fund's schedule, not at the next NAV every business day.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the interval fund with a listed closed-end fund. He does not sell the position on an exchange this afternoon.
distractorExplanations.d: Locks the shares until a maturity date with no repurchase before then. An interval fund does repurchase, but on its schedule, not as a daily mutual fund and not as a hold-to-maturity bond.

prompt: Rita's variable annuity subaccount lost value last quarter. She asks whether the insurer's general account absorbs that loss. The investment risk:

options.text: Moves to the general account, which insures the subaccount against a market decline
Is pooled with the insurer's fixed annuities in the general account, the same way a fixed contract credits interest
Remains in the separate account and is not absorbed by the insurer's general account
Ends when the premium is paid, because the insurer then promises the separate-account value will not fall

explanation: In a variable annuity the investment risk of the subaccounts sits in the separate account. The contract owner bears that market risk. The insurer's general account backs the insurer's fixed obligations; it does not absorb a decline in the separate account or insure the subaccount against a loss.

distractorExplanations.a: Moves the market loss into the general account. The separate account, not the general account, holds the variable subaccounts and their investment risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Mixes the variable contract with a fixed annuity. Fixed interest is a general-account feature; Rita's subaccount loss stays in the separate account.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the paid premium as the end of investment risk. Paying the premium does not stop the separate account from falling.

prompt: Carlos is still paying into a variable annuity and has not annuitized. He asks which units he holds now and which units he will hold after annuitization. He holds:

options.text: Annuity units during the pay-in period, and accumulation units after he annuitizes
Accumulation units both before and after annuitization, because the unit name stays the same when payments begin
Annuity units from the first premium, so there is no separate accumulation-unit stage before he annuitizes
Accumulation units during the pay-in period, and annuity units after he annuitizes

explanation: During the accumulation, or pay-in, period, a variable annuity is measured in accumulation units. When the owner annuitizes, those units convert to annuity units, which determine the variable payments. The names are not interchangeable, and annuity units do not exist from the first premium.

distractorExplanations.a: Swaps the two units. Accumulation units are the pay-in measure; annuity units come after annuitization, not before.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeps accumulation units after payments start. Annuitization converts the contract to annuity units.
distractorExplanations.c: Starts the contract in annuity units. The pay-in period uses accumulation units; annuity units follow annuitization.

prompt: During the accumulation period, Elena asks whether the death benefit on her variable annuity is the cash she would receive if she surrendered today. Those two figures:

options.text: Are different contract amounts: the death benefit is not the surrender cash she could take out today
Are the same figure, because the death benefit is defined as the check a surrender would pay her today
Trade places after the first contract year, so the surrender value is relabeled as the death benefit
Are both general-account floors, so neither one can sit below the premiums she has paid into the contract

explanation: During accumulation, the death benefit is the amount payable to beneficiaries under the contract. It is not the cash surrender value Elena can take today. A surrender charge can reduce the check a living surrender produces, and the death benefit follows its own contract formula. The representative should not read one figure as the other.

distractorExplanations.b: Defines the death benefit as today's surrender check. The death benefit and the amount she can surrender today are different contract figures.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the labels after year one. The death benefit does not become the surrender value because a contract anniversary passed.
distractorExplanations.d: Puts both figures in the general account as a floor under premiums. The separate-account contract does not make the surrender check and the death benefit the same guaranteed premium balance.

prompt: Paul uses a Section 1035 exchange to move one deferred annuity directly into another deferred annuity. On current income tax and the old surrender charge, the exchange:

options.text: Cancels the surrender charge, because the tax code treats the old contract as if that charge did not apply
Can avoid current income tax on a direct transfer between insurers and still leave the surrender charge in place
Taxes the full account as income this year, and it also leaves the old surrender charge in place on top of that tax
Becomes free of current income tax after he surrenders for cash and mails his own check to the new insurer

explanation: A qualifying Section 1035 exchange can move a deferred annuity into another deferred annuity without current income tax, if the transfer goes directly between insurers. The exchange does not erase a surrender charge on the old contract. That charge can still be deducted from the amount that moves. Cashing out and sending a personal check is not a 1035 exchange.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the tax-free transfer to cancel the surrender charge. Section 1035 addresses current income tax on a proper exchange; it does not waive the old contract's surrender charge.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxes the account now. A direct 1035 exchange of one deferred annuity for another is not a currently taxable surrender.
distractorExplanations.d: Allows Paul to take the cash and write a check. Constructive receipt of the proceeds is not a 1035 exchange and can trigger current income tax.

prompt: Diane owns a variable life policy and asks whether its cash value works like the scheduled cash value of fixed whole life. Compared with fixed whole life, that cash value:

options.text: Follows a fixed schedule, so a decline in the separate account cannot reduce the cash she has built
Rises when the separate account falls, because the general account offsets that drop dollar for dollar
Moves with the separate account she chose and is not the scheduled cash value of a whole-life policy
Equals the policy death benefit, so a drop in the separate account does not change the cash she can access

explanation: Variable life cash value moves with the separate account the policy owner selected. It is not the scheduled, guaranteed cash value of fixed whole life, and the general account does not credit it on a fixed table. A decline in the separate account can reduce the cash value. Cash value and the death benefit are not the same number.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives variable life the fixed cash-value schedule of whole life. The separate account can reduce Diane's cash value.
distractorExplanations.b: Has the general account offset a separate-account decline dollar for dollar. Variable life cash value moves with the separate account; the general account does not fill that gap.
distractorExplanations.d: Equates cash value with the death benefit. The cash value she can access is the separate-account value, not the death benefit itself.

prompt: A parent owns a 529 plan. The child, who is the beneficiary, asks to name a younger sibling as the new beneficiary. Who controls that change?

options.text: The child, because the beneficiary becomes the owner of a 529 once the account is opened for college
The college named on the application, which must approve a new beneficiary before the plan will retitle the account
The fund manager inside the plan, who may retitle the beneficiary when the child sends a written request
The parent who owns the 529 plan, rather than the child who is named only as the beneficiary of that plan

explanation: The owner of a 529 controls the account, including a change of beneficiary. The child who is the beneficiary does not own the account and does not control that change. The college named in the paperwork and the plan's investment manager do not take the owner's place.

distractorExplanations.a: Hands control to the beneficiary child. Opening a 529 for college does not make the child the owner, so the child cannot direct the beneficiary change.
distractorExplanations.b: Gives the college a veto over the title. A 529 beneficiary change is the account owner's decision, not the school's.
distractorExplanations.c: Lets the fund manager retitle the account at the child's request. The manager runs the investments; the owner controls the beneficiary.

prompt: A city treasurer asks whether a local government investment pool is something the city can use the way a family uses a 529 for college bills. An LGIP is:

options.text: A municipal fund security that state and local governments use for public cash, not a 529 for a family's college bills
A 529 the treasurer opens with the city as the student and the city's operating budget as the qualified college expense
A municipal bond the city buys and sells in the secondary market, with the representative soliciting those bond trades
An open-end corporate bond fund the city buys at the public offering price when it wants a college-style account for employees

explanation: A local government investment pool is a municipal fund security used by state and local governments to invest public funds. It is not a 529 plan, which is the retail municipal fund security a family uses for education. The treasurer is not opening a college account, and the pool is not a secondary-market municipal bond or a corporate bond fund.

distractorExplanations.b: Relabels the LGIP as a 529 for the city. A 529 is a family's education account; an LGIP is a government pool, not a college plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the pool into a municipal bond traded in the secondary market. An LGIP is a municipal fund security, not a muni bond solicitation.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes an open-end corporate bond fund. The product the treasurer asked about is a government investment pool, not a corporate bond fund.

prompt: Leah reinvests a mutual fund dividend in a taxable account and says the new shares must be tax-free because no cash reached her bank. That reinvestment:

options.text: Is tax-free, because a dividend she did not receive in cash is not a distribution from the fund
Usually buys new shares at NAV, and the reinvested dividend is still taxable in a taxable account
Carries a new front-end sales charge, as if the reinvested dividend were a fresh Class A purchase on the ticket
Must be paid in cash, because an open-end fund does not issue new shares when a shareholder reinvests a dividend

explanation: Mutual fund dividends that are reinvested are usually used to buy new shares at NAV, without a new front-end sales charge. In a taxable account the dividend is still income for the year it is paid. Skipping the cash payment does not make the dividend tax-free.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a reinvested dividend as if it were not a distribution. The shareholder is taxed on the dividend in a taxable account even when the shares are purchased with it.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a front-end sales charge to the reinvestment. Dividend reinvestment is usually executed at NAV, not at a new Class A public offering price.
distractorExplanations.d: Says the fund cannot issue shares for a reinvested dividend. Reinvestment is a normal mutual fund feature; the tax point is that the dividend is still taxable.

prompt: Chris receives the summary prospectus. The representative then describes the fund with a short sales slogan about fees and the objective. The fees and objective that govern are:

options.text: The slogan's wording, because delivery of the summary prospectus replaces the statutory prospectus and its fee table
The slogan's fee quote, while the objective may be restated to match the result Chris says he wants from the fund
The fees and the investment objective stated in the statutory prospectus itself, not the version in a sales slogan
Still open until Chris signs, so the representative may revise both the fees and the objective in the conversation before the ticket is entered

explanation: A summary prospectus is a standardized summary that can be delivered when the statutory prospectus is available. The fund's fees and investment objective remain the ones in the statutory prospectus. A sales slogan does not replace that disclosure, and the representative cannot rewrite either item to fit the conversation.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the summary prospectus as a replacement that lets the slogan control. The summary does not make a sales line the fund's fees or objective.
distractorExplanations.b: Lets the slogan set the fee and lets the client's wish reset the objective. Both must match the statutory prospectus, not the pitch or the hope.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaves fees and the objective unset until the signature. They are already stated in the statutory prospectus and are not revised orally.

prompt: Imani wants to leave a unit investment trust and asks whether she must find a buyer on an exchange, the way a closed-end fund shareholder would. The trust:

options.text: Is exchange-traded like a closed-end fund, so she has to sell her units to another investor at the market
Refuses redemptions until the termination date, and the sponsor will not take the units back before then
Is a managed open-end fund, so a portfolio manager sells bonds in the market the same day to raise her cash
Redeems her units directly with the trust, rather than selling those units to a buyer on an exchange now

explanation: A unit investment trust is redeemable with the trust. Imani does not have to find a buyer on an exchange the way a shareholder of a traditional closed-end fund does. The trust is also not an open-end fund with a manager selling bonds to meet her redemption.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the UIT with a closed-end fund. Closed-end shares are sold on an exchange; UIT units are redeemed with the trust.
distractorExplanations.b: Locks the units until termination. The trust redeems units during its life; she is not required to wait for the end date to exit.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the trust into a managed open-end fund. A UIT has a fixed portfolio, and the redemption is with the trust rather than a manager trading the book that day.

prompt: Greg bought an open-end growth fund. He asks the representative to describe the objective as capital preservation because that is the result he hopes for. The representative should:

options.text: Describe the prospectus growth objective, and not replace it with capital preservation because that is the result he wants
Relabel the fund as capital preservation on the account form if Greg writes that goal down and initials the change
Use whichever objective sounds safer in the conversation, because the prospectus objective is a sales suggestion the representative may soften
Promise that the growth fund will preserve capital if Greg holds the shares through a full year and does not redeem early

explanation: The representative describes an open-end fund's objective from the prospectus. A growth fund seeks capital appreciation. The client's hope does not convert that objective into capital preservation, and a note on the account form does not amend the prospectus. The representative should not promise a result the fund's objective does not state.

distractorExplanations.b: Lets an initialed account form replace the prospectus objective. The growth objective stays what the prospectus says, even if Greg writes a different goal.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the prospectus objective as a slogan the representative may soften. The objective to describe is the one in the prospectus, not a safer-sounding substitute.
distractorExplanations.d: Promises capital preservation from a growth fund if the holding period is long enough. Time in the fund does not change a growth objective into capital preservation.

prompt: Nina is buying a mutual fund class with no front-end load, so the purchase is filled at NAV. She asks if the representative adds a commission on top of that NAV. A contingent deferred sales charge:

options.text: Is added on top of NAV at purchase, even though the class shows no front-end load on the confirmation
Is collected on her early redemption and is not a commission stacked on NAV at the time of purchase
Replaces the fund's expense ratio and is billed once a year as the fund's operating cost instead of a sales charge
Is a prospectus label rather than a charge collected when she redeems before the schedule runs off

explanation: A contingent deferred sales charge is paid when the client redeems during the period the charge still applies. On a class with no front-end load, the purchase is made at NAV. The representative does not add a commission on top of that NAV. The charge is not the fund's annual expense ratio, and it is collected if she leaves early.

distractorExplanations.a: Stacks the contingent deferred sales charge on NAV at purchase. That charge is an exit charge, not a commission added to a no-front-load purchase.
distractorExplanations.c: Replaces the expense ratio with the contingent deferred sales charge. The expense ratio is the fund's annual operating cost; the CDSC is a sales charge on an early redemption.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the charge as disclosure that is never collected. If she redeems while the schedule still applies, the contingent deferred sales charge is paid.

prompt: Brooke can place a larger purchase in one fund family and qualify for a breakpoint. She asks the representative to split that order on purpose across two unrelated fund families. The split:

options.text: Still receives the breakpoint, because unrelated families combine her tickets into one sales-charge discount
Earns a deeper discount than one family would give, because each sponsor matches the other family's lower sales charge
Can miss that family's breakpoint, because purchases at unrelated fund families are not combined for the sales charge
Is how a breakpoint is earned, because a purchase that stays inside a single family is not eligible for the lower sales charge

explanation: A breakpoint is a lower sales charge on a larger purchase inside one fund family. Purchases at two unrelated families are not added together for that breakpoint. Splitting the order on purpose can leave each ticket on the higher sales charge the smaller amount pays. The discount follows the family, not a pair of unrelated sponsors.

distractorExplanations.a: Combines unrelated fund families into one breakpoint. A breakpoint applies within a family; the other sponsor's purchase does not count.
distractorExplanations.b: Claims two sponsors will each grant a deeper discount. Unrelated families do not match each other's sales charge to create a larger breakpoint.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the family rule. The lower sales charge is for a larger purchase in one family, not for an order that is split away from that family.

prompt: Victor is offered a variable annuity living-benefit rider and is told it means the separate account cannot fall. Before he adds the rider, he should understand that it:

options.text: Guarantees the separate-account value itself cannot decline, and the rider is included at no extra cost
Moves the subaccounts into the general account, which then guarantees principal the way a fixed annuity credits a set rate
Removes both the rider charge and the surrender charge for as long as he keeps this contract in force
Carries a separate fee and contractual limits, and it does not stop the separate-account value from falling

explanation: A living-benefit rider has a fee and operates inside the contract's limits, such as a benefit base or a withdrawal formula that is not the same thing as account value. The separate account can still decline. The rider does not move the subaccounts into the general account, and it does not promise that the investments themselves cannot fall.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the rider into a free floor under the separate-account value. The account can fall, and the rider has a cost.
distractorExplanations.b: Converts the variable contract into a fixed annuity. A living-benefit rider does not transfer the subaccounts to the general account.
distractorExplanations.c: Cancels the rider fee and the surrender charge. Adding the rider does not erase either charge.

prompt: A parent asks for a 529 plan for college savings. The representative starts describing a municipal bond that trades in the secondary market. A 529 plan:

options.text: Is a municipal fund security for college savings, not a secondary-market municipal bond a Series 6 representative may solicit
Is a municipal bond, so the representative may solicit that secondary-market bond trade for the parent under a Series 6 registration
Trades through the day at a premium or a discount, like a closed-end municipal fund the parent would buy or sell in the aftermarket
Is an individual bond the parent holds to maturity, issued in the child's name, with the college acting as the bond issuer

explanation: A 529 plan is a municipal fund security. It is not a municipal bond, and a Series 6 representative is not soliciting a secondary-market municipal bond when the parent asks for a 529. The plan is also not an exchange-traded closed-end fund and not a single bond issued by a college in the child's name.

distractorExplanations.b: Calls the 529 a municipal bond and puts a secondary-market bond solicitation under Series 6. A 529 is a municipal fund security, not that bond trade.
distractorExplanations.c: Gives the 529 an aftermarket premium or discount like a closed-end fund. The parent is not buying or selling a closed-end municipal fund on an exchange.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the plan into one bond issued by the college to the child. A 529 is an account in a municipal fund security, not a single bond the parent holds to maturity.

prompt: Sofia subtracts a fund's NAV from its public offering price and tells her representative that the gap is the fund's annual expense ratio. The sales load:

options.text: Is the expense ratio, because the gap and the fund's yearly operating costs are the same charge under two labels
Is the 12b-1 fee, so the gap between the offering price and NAV is the annual trail the fund pays the representative
Is the public offering price minus NAV, and that sales-load gap is not the same thing as the annual expense ratio
Is a market premium, the same idea as a closed-end fund trading above NAV in the secondary market after its offering

explanation: The sales load is the difference between the public offering price and NAV. As a percent of the offering price, the sales charge is that difference divided by the public offering price. The annual expense ratio is the fund's operating expenses, including items such as management fees and 12b-1 fees, measured against assets. The load and the expense ratio are different charges.

distractorExplanations.a: Equates the sales load with the expense ratio. The gap between the offering price and NAV is the sales load; the expense ratio is the fund's annual operating cost.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls that gap the 12b-1 fee. A 12b-1 fee is an ongoing fund expense inside the expense ratio, not the one-time difference between the offering price and NAV.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the load as a closed-end market premium. On an open-end purchase the gap is the sales load built into the public offering price, not an aftermarket premium.

prompt: Regulation Best Interest is built on which four component obligations?

options.text: Disclosure, suitability, pricing, and supervision
Disclosure, care, conflict of interest, compliance
Know your customer, care, fair pricing, and loyalty
Disclosure, best execution, suitability, and training

explanation: Reg BI requires broker-dealers to meet a disclosure obligation, a care obligation, a conflict-of-interest obligation, and a compliance obligation when recommending securities to retail customers.

distractorExplanations.a: Reg BI's components are disclosure, care, conflict of interest, and compliance; pricing is not one of them.
distractorExplanations.c: Fair pricing and loyalty are not the named Reg BI obligations.
distractorExplanations.d: Best execution and training are separate FINRA duties, not Reg BI components.

Combining family accounts to reach a lower sales charge

distractorExplanations.a: The violation is failing to help the client reach a discount, not saving them money.

prompt: Ella, 74, holds a variable annuity bought four years ago. A rep proposes a 1035 exchange into a new VA with a richer living-benefit rider and a new 7-year surrender schedule. Ella may need $40,000 for home care next year. Best course?

options.text: Proceed, because a 1035 exchange is tax-free and therefore suitable
Proceed if Ella signs a form acknowledging the new surrender charges
Proceed, because the richer rider better protects her lifetime income
Advise against it, given the new surrender period and her cash need

explanation: Under FINRA Rule 2330 an exchange must be suitable after weighing surrender charges, benefits lost and gained, and the customer's liquidity needs. A fresh 7-year surrender schedule conflicts with Ella's expected $40,000 withdrawal, so the rider does not justify the switch.

distractorExplanations.a: Section 1035 avoids current tax on the exchange, but tax-free treatment says nothing about whether new surrender charges fit her needs.

distractorExplanations.c: Focuses on the rider and ignores that a new 7-year surrender schedule would penalize the withdrawal she expects next year.

Mostly money market funds for liquidity

prompt: Tax-efficient placement often suggests holding

options.text: Municipal bonds inside a traditional IRA
Tax-efficient index funds in tax-deferred accounts
High-yield bonds in a taxable brokerage account
Tax-inefficient assets in tax-advantaged accounts

explanation: Asset location: put tax-inefficient exposures in sheltered accounts when it helps.

distractorExplanations.a: Munis are already tax-exempt, so holding them in an IRA wastes the benefit.

prompt: Nora Chen asks for a fund idea in a taxable account. Her representative has not read the prospectus and cannot describe the fund's objective, principal risks, or costs, yet still recommends the firm's international growth fund. Which judgment is correct?

options.text: The recommendation fails reasonable-basis suitability, because this fund's objective, risks, and costs were never reviewed.
Sending Nora the prospectus after she buys cures the gap, because she can read the objective and risks the representative skipped.
