explanation: Reasonable-basis suitability requires the representative, after reasonable diligence, to understand the security and to have a reasonable basis that it could suit at least some investors. Recommending a fund without knowing its objective, risks, and costs fails that component. Reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability are the three suitability components, and this miss is the first of them.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses prospectus delivery to the customer with the representative's own duty to understand the fund before recommending it.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the sponsor's reputation as a substitute for reading this fund's objective, risks, and costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates the sequence: reasonable-basis suitability applies before the fund is matched to Nora, and an unread prospectus fails it.

prompt: Malik Adeyemi is gathering a house down payment he expects to spend in about two years. His representative recommends putting that entire sum in a small-cap growth mutual fund because Malik is 34 and says he can live with swings. What should the representative conclude?

options.text: The fund fits, because two years is long enough for a small-cap growth strategy to work through a decline.
That house down payment does not belong in the small-cap growth fund when he needs the cash in about two years.
Customer-specific suitability looks at age and his remark about swings, so the house date drops out of the analysis.
Buy the fund if its long-term record looks strong, because that record shows the down payment will be on hand at closing.

explanation: Customer-specific suitability matches the product to this customer's time horizon and liquidity need. A house down payment due in about two years can be lost or unavailable in a small-cap growth fund. Age and a comment that he can live with swings do not lengthen the date he needs the cash. That component is separate from reasonable-basis suitability and quantitative suitability.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a two-year spending date as a long enough recovery window for a volatile small-cap growth fund.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops the house date out of customer-specific suitability and substitutes age plus a comment about swings.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses a past performance record as if it guaranteed that the down payment will be available when the house closes.

prompt: Over eight months a representative moves Priya Shah among four bond mutual funds. Each ticket is small, and each new fund is a plausible bond holding for her. The switches keep creating new sales charges. How is the pattern judged?

options.text: Judge each switch alone, because a run of small, plausible bond-fund tickets cannot be excessive.
Skip this review, because a quantitative look applies to stock trading and not to mutual fund switches.
The pattern can still fail quantitative suitability, because the repeated sales charges make the switches excessive.
Ignore the repeated sales charges, because every replacement fund stayed inside the bond allocation Priya had already accepted.

explanation: Quantitative suitability looks at the series of recommended transactions together, not ticket by ticket. A string of fund switches can fail that component when the pattern is excessive in frequency and cost, even though each ticket is small and each bond fund would have been plausible on its own. Small size does not answer the series question.

distractorExplanations.a: Judges each small ticket in isolation and misses that quantitative suitability reviews whether the pattern of switches is excessive.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses quantitative suitability with a stock-trading rule and wrongly exempts a series of mutual fund switches.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats staying inside a bond allocation as if it erased repeated sales charges on an excessive pattern of switches.

prompt: Helen Park's new-account form shows a modest pension, little savings beyond this account, and a goal of keeping principal available. On the call she says she feels brave today and asks for a sector equity fund. What should guide the representative?

options.text: Today's remark that she feels brave, because a fresh comment on risk replaces the financial facts already on the form.
The sector fund she named, because asking for a product means she has accepted the principal loss that fund can produce.
The pension by itself, because any guaranteed income proves she can bear a loss in the rest of the account.
Her ability to bear a loss, based on thin savings and principal that must stay available, rather than today's mood.

explanation: Ability to bear loss is financial capacity: income, other savings, liquidity, and whether principal has to stay available. Helen's statement that she feels brave today is a mood, not that capacity. Customer-specific suitability uses the profile. A sector equity fund can lose principal she has already said she needs to keep.

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes a same-day comment about feeling brave for the financial facts that measure her ability to bear a loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a product request as proof she can afford the principal loss, which is a different question from wanting the fund.
distractorExplanations.c: Equates a modest pension with capacity to lose the rest of the account and ignores thin savings and the liquidity goal.

prompt: George Okonkwo, 79, owns a variable annuity. A caller the representative has never verified says George wants the contract surrendered today and the proceeds wired to a new account. George is not on the line. What is the appropriate step?

options.text: Escalate, and do not surrender the contract the same day, because this caller has not been verified to act for him.
Surrender the contract today, because a caller who can quote the account number may liquidate a variable annuity.
Wire the proceeds if the caller knows the contract number and George's birth date, which together authorize the surrender.
Replace the request with a 1035 exchange into a new variable annuity so the wire is handled as a tax-free transfer.

explanation: A sudden request to liquidate a senior's variable annuity, made by a caller the representative has not verified, is an escalation. The firm should confirm who is directing the money and whether the owner is being pressured before anything leaves the contract. Processing a same-day surrender on an unverified call skips that check. Quoting account facts is not authority to surrender.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats knowledge of an account number as authority to surrender a senior's variable annuity the same day.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses two personal facts with verification of the caller's authority and with a completed exploitation review.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps an unverified liquidation for a 1035 exchange, which still moves the contract without confirming who is directing it.

prompt: Diego Morales will need his invested cash in a little over a year for a scheduled expense. A representative recommends a variable annuity whose surrender schedule runs well past that date. Why is the annuity a poor fit?

options.text: Age is the barrier that matters, so a short expense date does not make this variable annuity a poor fit.
The surrender schedule runs past the date he needs the cash, which is why this variable annuity is a poor fit.
The surrender schedule matters for equity subaccounts, and a bond subaccount would make the annuity suitable for the expense.
A surrender schedule is harmless when the client already knows the expense date, because the charge applies if the insurer cancels the contract.

explanation: Customer-specific suitability includes time horizon and liquidity. A variable annuity whose surrender schedule runs past the date the client needs the money is a poor fit: he may have to pay to reach cash that should have stayed accessible. Choosing a bond subaccount does not erase the surrender charge, and the charge is not limited to a cancellation by the insurer.

distractorExplanations.a: Replaces the mismatch between a short expense date and a long surrender schedule with an age test the facts do not raise.
distractorExplanations.c: Blames the subaccount type and misses that the surrender charge can apply whichever investment option he picks.
distractorExplanations.d: Misstates how a surrender charge works by tying it to the insurer canceling, rather than to the client taking money out early.

prompt: Lena Brooks wants her entire brokerage account in a single energy-sector mutual fund. She has no other investments. The fund matches a high risk tolerance she wrote on the form. What suitability problem remains?

options.text: None remains, because a sector fund already spreads her money across the companies inside that industry.
None remains once the form shows high risk tolerance, which replaces any need to spread the account across sectors.
The whole account is concentrated in one sector, and marking a high risk tolerance does not remove that bet.
The open issue is quantitative suitability, because holding one fund is treated as an excessive series of transactions.

explanation: Customer-specific suitability includes concentration. One sector fund as the entire account ties Lena's results to a single industry. Holdings of many companies inside that industry do not remove the sector bet, and a high risk-tolerance mark does not erase it. Quantitative suitability is about a series of transactions, not about this single concentrated position.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses diversification across companies in one industry with diversification across sectors.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a high risk-tolerance answer as a waiver of concentration in a single sector fund.
distractorExplanations.d: Mislabels a one-fund concentration problem as quantitative suitability, which reviews a series of transactions.

prompt: Samir Haddad may need part of his cash next month for a medical bill. A representative suggests an interval fund that does not redeem shares daily and offers to repurchase only a limited amount on a periodic schedule. Why is that a poor place for this cash?

options.text: Interval funds are unsuitable for every retail investor, no matter when the investor needs the cash.
A credit interval fund can be redeemed in full on demand next month, so the liquidity worry is limited to equity portfolios.
Liquidity is not the issue, because an interval fund's repurchase offer works like an open-end mutual fund's daily redemption.
He may not be able to take the cash out next month, because an interval fund does not redeem shares on demand.

explanation: An interval fund does not redeem shares every business day. It periodically offers to repurchase a limited portion of shares, so cash the client may need next month can be unavailable. Customer-specific suitability includes that liquidity need. The limit is a feature of the interval structure, not a quirk of equity portfolios, and it is not the same as an open-end mutual fund redemption.

distractorExplanations.a: Overstates the rule by barring interval funds for every retail investor instead of matching them to someone who does not need the cash soon.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents daily, full redemption for a credit interval fund; the repurchase limit is not an equity-only feature.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an interval fund's limited periodic repurchase offer with an open-end mutual fund's daily redemption.

prompt: Renee Walsh expects to hold one mutual fund for many years and can buy either Class A or Class C. Class A charges a front-end sales load and has lower ongoing expenses. Class C has no front-end load and higher ongoing expenses. Nobody has computed a dollar crossover. Which point is fair?

options.text: Over a long hold, Class A can cost less than Class C, because the front-end sales charge is paid once and ongoing expenses are lower.
Class C is the cheaper long-term choice whenever the front-end load is absent, so higher ongoing expenses cannot change the result.
Quote a dollar amount at which Class A becomes cheaper, even though none was calculated, and call that figure the fund's breakpoint.
Share class does not matter on a long horizon, because both classes own the same portfolio and the sponsor pays the extra ongoing expenses.

explanation: For a long holding period, Class A can be the lower-cost share class versus Class C: the front-end charge is paid once, and ongoing expenses are lower. The representative should compare this client's horizon with the actual schedule in the prospectus and should not invent a dollar crossover or relabel a made-up figure as a breakpoint. Cost is part of the care analysis.

distractorExplanations.b: Stops the comparison at the missing front-end load and ignores the higher ongoing expenses that can make Class C cost more over a long hold.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a dollar crossover and misnames it as a breakpoint, which is a sales-charge tier in the prospectus, not a made-up figure.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes the sponsor pays the share-class expense difference, when those ongoing costs are borne by the shareholder.

prompt: Jonah Ellis already owns a balanced mutual fund. He asks whether he should stay in it. His representative reviews the profile and tells him to keep the fund rather than switch. Jonah says that cannot be a recommendation because he is not buying anything new. Which reply is right?

options.text: Jonah is right that no recommendation occurred, because he is not buying a new fund or adding cash.
Telling him to keep the fund is still a hold recommendation, even though he is not buying any new shares.
It becomes a recommendation if the representative also names a second fund in the same conversation.
Hold instructions sit outside suitability and Regulation Best Interest, which cover purchases and exchanges.

explanation: A recommendation to hold is still a recommendation. Suitability and the Regulation Best Interest care obligation cover explicit advice to buy, sell, or hold. Telling Jonah to keep the balanced fund, after reviewing his profile, is hold advice and needs a basis in the customer and the product. The fact that no new shares are purchased does not take that advice outside the rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Limits the word recommendation to a new purchase or added cash and misses an explicit instruction to hold.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a requirement that a second fund be named before hold advice counts as a recommendation.
distractorExplanations.d: Confines suitability and Regulation Best Interest to purchases and exchanges, leaving out an explicit hold recommendation.

prompt: A representative's full case for recommending a mutual fund to Luis Ortega is that she has preferred that fund family for years. She does not discuss the fund's risks, costs, or Luis's objective. Has she satisfied the Regulation Best Interest care obligation?

options.text: Yes. Years of preferring one fund family are the diligence the care obligation requires.
Yes, when the family is widely known, because that reputation replaces a look at this customer's objective and the fund's costs.
No. A favorite fund family is not the care analysis of this fund's risks, costs, and Luis's objective.
Yes, once she tells Luis she likes the family, because that disclosure completes the care obligation.

explanation: The Regulation Best Interest care obligation is not satisfied by naming the fund family the representative likes. Care requires an understanding of the particular fund's risks, rewards, and costs, and a match to this retail customer. A familiar brand does not do that work, and disclosing the preference does not replace it. Disclosure is a separate obligation from care.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a long-standing preference for a fund family as the product diligence the care obligation requires.
distractorExplanations.b: Substitutes brand recognition for a customer-specific look at Luis's objective and the fund's costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses disclosing a preference with satisfying the care obligation, which still requires the product and customer analysis.

prompt: Chris Daley pays very little income tax, and the profile lists no education savings goal. A representative recommends a 529 plan solely because the brochure calls the plan tax-advantaged. Chris asks whether that label is enough. What should the representative conclude?

options.text: The label is enough, because a tax-advantaged education account is suitable for any retail customer who can open one.
Very little tax makes the 529 a stronger fit, because tax-advantaged products are built for customers who pay little income tax.
The brochure wording is enough, and an education goal can be written onto the profile after the 529 is funded.
The tax-advantaged brochure label does not by itself make the 529 suitable for Chris, who has no education goal.

explanation: A 529 is not automatically suitable because a brochure says it is tax-advantaged. Customer-specific suitability still asks whether this customer has an education purpose, a fitting time horizon, and a tax situation in which the tax feature matters. Someone who pays very little income tax may get little benefit from tax-free growth, so the label is not a reason by itself. No tax bracket has to be assumed to see that gap.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the tax-advantaged label as if it made a 529 suitable for any retail customer who is allowed to open one.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the tax point by treating a very low tax situation as the reason a tax-advantaged 529 is suitable.
distractorExplanations.c: Lets brochure wording stand in for suitability and postpones the missing education goal until after the account is funded.

prompt: Ruth Stein's risk questionnaire, completed this week, selects preservation of capital. Her representative sets the form aside and recommends an aggressive growth mutual fund, calling the questionnaire paperwork. What is wrong?

options.text: The recommendation ignores the preservation-of-capital objective Ruth just selected on this week's questionnaire.
Nothing is wrong, because a risk questionnaire is optional paperwork and does not constrain the funds that may be recommended.
The miss is that preservation of capital can be met with a bond fund and with no other category of mutual fund.
The questionnaire starts to control the account after she has held the growth fund through a full market cycle.

explanation: A current questionnaire that selects preservation of capital is part of the customer profile. Customer-specific suitability requires the recommendation to fit that objective. Setting the form aside and recommending an aggressive growth fund, which can lose principal, ignores the profile she just completed. Preservation of capital does not mean the single permitted product is a bond fund; it does mean this growth fund is a mismatch.

distractorExplanations.b: Dismisses a completed risk questionnaire as optional paperwork that suitability can ignore.
distractorExplanations.c: Overstates the objective by claiming a bond fund is the single category that can pursue preservation of capital.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays the profile until after a market cycle in the aggressive growth fund, which is the purchase the objective rejects.

prompt: Owen Clarke is about to add money inside a mutual fund family where a breakpoint would lower the sales charge on the new purchase. His representative instead moves him to a different family. The reason discussed is that the new family pays the representative a fresh sales charge. What is the harm?

options.text: There is no harm, because the representative may move a customer to a new fund family whenever a new sales charge is available.
The switch drops an available breakpoint in the current family so the representative can earn a new sales charge.
The harm is tax, because a breakpoint is a tax credit the customer loses by leaving the old family.
This cannot be a switching problem, because breakpoints exist for variable annuities and not for mutual fund families.

explanation: Moving the client to a new fund family solely so the representative earns a new sales charge, when a breakpoint was available in the old family, is a switching harm. The representative should consider the breakpoint the additional purchase could reach before recommending a change that costs the customer more. A breakpoint is a reduced sales charge inside the fund family, not a tax credit.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a new sales charge for the representative as a sufficient reason to leave a family where a breakpoint was available.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels a breakpoint as a tax credit instead of a reduction in the mutual fund sales charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Denies that mutual fund families offer breakpoints and confines the switching problem to variable annuities.

prompt: In the meeting, Andre Wallace says his priority is preservation of capital for money he cannot afford to lose. The representative keeps pitching an aggressive growth fund and asks Andre to sign the purchase form before he leaves. What should happen instead?

options.text: Have him sign now, because a recent rise in the growth fund overrides the preservation goal he stated in the meeting.
Proceed based on age, because preservation of capital applies after the customer has retired and not before.
Refuse the signature, because the aggressive growth fund fights the preservation-of-capital goal he just stated.
Move the same dollars into a variable annuity and skip the surrender discussion, because an insurance wrapper preserves capital.

explanation: Andre has said he needs preservation of capital for money he cannot afford to lose. An aggressive growth fund can decline in value, so pushing him to sign is a customer-specific mismatch. Recent performance and age do not replace the objective he stated. A variable annuity is not a capital-preservation shortcut, and its surrender charges and market risk would need their own review.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets a recent rise in the growth fund override the preservation-of-capital priority Andre stated in the meeting.
distractorExplanations.b: Confines preservation of capital to retired customers and ignores the objective he stated for this money.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a variable annuity wrapper as proof of capital preservation and skips the surrender charges and market risk.

prompt: The new-account profile on file belongs to Sofia Marin alone. She did not ask for a joint account, and no second owner has been identified or profiled. The representative opens a joint account because the joint form is the faster ticket to enter. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing is wrong if Sofia is married, because a spouse becomes a joint owner as soon as one profile is on file.
The joint form is appropriate when it is faster to enter, because registration is an operations step and not part of suitability.
Open the joint account now and collect the second owner's profile after the first trade is placed.
Do not open a joint account from Sofia's profile alone, because no second owner has been identified or profiled.

explanation: The profile is one person's, and a joint account has two owners. Opening the joint registration because the form is faster puts the wrong account type on the ticket and skips the second owner's identity, authority, and suitability information. Marriage does not make a spouse a joint owner by default. The account type has to match the people who will actually own it.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats marriage as automatic joint ownership once a single profile is on file.
distractorExplanations.b: Reduces account registration to a speed choice and removes it from the customer record the recommendation depends on.
distractorExplanations.c: Opens the joint account and places a trade before the second owner has been identified or profiled.

prompt: A representative wants authority to switch Nina Petrov among mutual funds without calling her before each choice. Nina says "go ahead" on the phone about today's idea. No written discretionary authorization is on file, and the firm has not accepted one. May that oral comment be treated as discretion to switch funds?

options.text: No. Choosing the next mutual fund for Nina is discretion and must be in writing that the firm has already accepted.
Yes. Her oral go-ahead is the written discretionary authorization the firm would otherwise accept before the switches.
Yes, if a follow-up email lists the funds after the switches, because that note makes the oral grant retroactive.
The writing requirement covers variable annuity exchanges, so mutual fund switches may run on oral discretion.

explanation: A discretionary fund switch needs prior written authorization that the firm has accepted before the representative uses it. An oral "go ahead" about today's idea is not that document. A later email does not create retroactive discretion, and the writing requirement is not limited to variable annuity exchanges. Approval of one fully described trade is an order; it is not ongoing authority to pick the funds.

distractorExplanations.b: Equates an oral go-ahead with the prior written discretionary authorization the firm must accept.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a follow-up email after the switches as if it created discretionary authority retroactively.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits the writing requirement to variable annuity exchanges and allows oral discretion for mutual fund switches.

prompt: Frank Doyle's account profile was completed three years ago, while he was working and listing growth as his objective. He tells the representative he retired last month. The representative is ready to recommend a new stock mutual fund from the old profile. What comes first?

options.text: Enter the growth-fund order, because a three-year-old profile stays current even after the customer reports a retirement.
Update Frank's profile to record the retirement he just reported, before any new fund recommendation.
Use the old growth objective, and refresh the file if Frank later complains about the recommendation.
Treat the retirement as an instruction to buy a variable annuity, and skip a new profile.

explanation: The profile is three years old, and Frank just retired. Retirement can change income, time horizon, liquidity, and the investment objective that was recorded while he was working. The representative should update the profile before a new recommendation. Customer-specific suitability depends on current information. Retirement itself does not select a variable annuity, and a complaint is not the trigger for an update the representative already knows is needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a three-year-old working-life profile as still current after the customer reports that he has retired.
distractorExplanations.c: Waits for a complaint before updating a profile the representative already knows is stale.
distractorExplanations.d: Reads retirement as a product selection for a variable annuity and skips the updated customer profile.

prompt: Paul Adebanjo sets aside cash he labels the emergency fund, the money to use if the household misses a paycheck. A representative recommends placing that cash in a variable annuity that still carries a surrender charge. Why does that fail?

options.text: It fails when the emergency fund exceeds the annuity's first purchase payment, because a smaller reserve is exempt from the charge.
It does not fail, because labeling a withdrawal an emergency waives the variable annuity surrender charge.
An emergency fund for a missed paycheck does not belong behind an annuity that still has a surrender charge.
It fails for equity subaccounts; the fixed account inside the same variable annuity is a proper emergency reserve.

explanation: An emergency fund has to be reachable when a paycheck stops. Putting it in a variable annuity that still has a surrender charge can cost the client, or block the client, for taking the reserve out. Customer-specific suitability includes that liquidity need. Calling the withdrawal an emergency does not by itself waive the charge, and a fixed account inside the contract does not remove the surrender schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a size exemption that would allow a smaller emergency fund to sit behind a surrender charge.
distractorExplanations.b: Assumes the surrender charge is waived automatically because the customer calls the withdrawal an emergency.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the fixed account inside the variable annuity as an emergency reserve and ignores the surrender charge on the contract.

prompt: Dana Cho owns a 529 plan for her teenage child. The child calls and asks the representative to move the 529 into a more aggressive portfolio. Dana has not requested the change and is not on the call. Who is the right party for that instruction?

options.text: The child, because a teenage beneficiary takes over investment direction on a 529.
Either the owner or the beneficiary, because a 529 makes them joint decision-makers for allocation changes.
The representative may switch the portfolio on the child's call and notify Dana after the trade.
Dana, the account owner, must direct any change; her child, the beneficiary, does not control the 529.

explanation: The parent owns the 529. The account owner, not the beneficiary child, directs investment changes. Recommending or entering a change the child asked for, without the owner, takes instructions from the wrong party. The representative should go back to Dana before any portfolio change. The child's age does not transfer that control.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives investment direction on the 529 to the teenage beneficiary, who is not the account owner.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the owner and the beneficiary as joint decision-makers for 529 allocation changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Lets the representative trade on the child's request and tell the owner afterward, which still skips the owner's instruction.

prompt: Each time a unit investment trust in Carl Ito's account reaches its scheduled end, and twice before that, his representative recommends another UIT. Every trust fits Carl's income objective, and each purchase is modest. New sales charges repeat. What can the series still fail?

options.text: Quantitative suitability can still fail on this series, because each new UIT purchase adds another sales charge.
Nothing fails, because quantitative suitability is met when each product would be acceptable on its own.
Reasonable-basis suitability is the component in play, because modest UIT purchases do not raise a quantitative problem.
Nothing fails when the objective is income, because that objective approves every later UIT the representative selects.

explanation: Several small switches that each look suitable can still fail quantitative suitability. That component reviews the series, including how often new sales charges are incurred, rather than stopping at the fact that one UIT matches an income objective. A reasonable-basis look at a single trust does not answer whether the pattern of rollovers is excessive.

distractorExplanations.b: Stops at each trust looking suitable and never asks whether the series of UIT sales charges is excessive.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigns the pattern to reasonable-basis suitability and denies that modest UIT purchases can raise quantitative suitability.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats an income objective as blanket approval for every subsequent UIT the representative wants to sell.

prompt: June Harlow, a public-school teacher, plans to retire in two years and says the money under discussion needs to produce income then. A representative recommends a variable annuity with a surrender schedule that runs well beyond those two years. What is the suitability result?

options.text: The annuity fits, because a teacher's pension makes the surrender schedule irrelevant to the retirement date.
A surrender schedule that runs past her retirement is a poor fit for the income she says she will need in two years.
The annuity fits if she picks a growth subaccount, since two years of growth will offset the cost of surrendering.
Match the retirement date for mutual funds; a variable annuity sold to a public-school employee is outside that horizon comparison.

explanation: A teacher two years from retirement who needs income then is not a candidate for a variable annuity with a surrender schedule that runs well past that date. Customer-specific suitability includes the horizon and the income need. A pension does not cancel the surrender charge on this contract, and a growth subaccount does not turn a near-term income need into a long lockup.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a teacher's pension as if it made the variable annuity's surrender schedule irrelevant to money needed at retirement.
distractorExplanations.c: Assumes two years of growth in a subaccount will offset the surrender cost and ignores the income timing.
distractorExplanations.d: Exempts a variable annuity sold to a school employee from the time-horizon match that applies to this recommendation.

prompt: A mutual fund prospectus states an objective of capital appreciation. Bea Laurent needs current income from the dollars she would invest. The representative still recommends the fund as her income vehicle. Which conclusion fits?

options.text: The fund is suitable for income, because capital appreciation and current income are interchangeable objectives in an open-end fund.
Reasonable-basis suitability for an income use is already met, because the same fund could suit some investors who want growth.
A capital-appreciation fund can suit a growth investor and is still the wrong vehicle for the current income Bea needs.
A distribution during the past year rewrites the prospectus objective, so the fund can be sold as an income vehicle.

explanation: This is a customer-specific miss, not a failure of reasonable-basis suitability. A capital-appreciation fund can still be suitable for some investors who want growth. It is the wrong vehicle for Bea, who needs current income. A past distribution does not rewrite the prospectus objective.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats capital appreciation and current income as interchangeable mutual fund objectives.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops once the fund could suit some growth investors and never tests the income use the representative is recommending.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a past distribution as a rewrite of the prospectus objective from capital appreciation to current income.

prompt: Two share classes of the same mutual fund are available to Evan Cho, and both fit his horizon. One costs him less. The representative recommends the class that pays the representative more and never mentions the cheaper class. What does that break?

options.text: No rule, because the representative may choose the share class that pays more whenever both classes can be sold.
Prospectus delivery, because a cost gap between share classes is not part of the recommendation itself.
Quantitative suitability, because picking one share class counts as an excessive series of transactions.
It breaks the care obligation by choosing what pays the representative more instead of the cheaper class.

explanation: When a lower-cost share class is available and suitable, choosing the class that pays the representative more, and not addressing the cheaper class, fails the care obligation. Cost is part of that analysis. Delivering a prospectus does not replace the comparison, and a single share-class choice is not the quantitative-suitability question of an excessive series of trades. No fee percentage is required to see the conflict.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats higher pay to the representative as a permitted basis for the share class when a lower-cost suitable class is available.
distractorExplanations.b: Reduces a share-class cost conflict to a prospectus-delivery item and leaves cost out of the recommendation.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels one share-class choice as quantitative suitability, which reviews a series of recommended transactions.

prompt: Anika Patel is a first-time investor. A representative wants to sell her a variable annuity with a complex living-benefit rider and has not determined whether Anika understands the rider's limits, costs, or the effect of withdrawals. What is required before that recommendation?

options.text: Establish that she understands the rider's limits, costs, and withdrawal effects before recommending it.
Nothing further, because a living-benefit rider makes the annuity suitable for every first-time investor.
A signature on the application is enough, because signing shows she understands the rider.
Replace the annuity with an aggressive sector fund, because a first-time investor has to start in equities.

explanation: A variable annuity with a complex living-benefit rider is a mismatch for a first-time investor unless the representative has established that the client understands it. The care obligation includes a reasonable basis to believe the customer grasps material features, including costs, limits, and how withdrawals affect the rider. A signature does not establish that understanding, and the rider does not make the contract suitable for every new investor.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the living-benefit rider as if it made the variable annuity suitable for every first-time investor without an understanding check.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a signature on the application with a determination that Anika understands the rider's limits and costs.
distractorExplanations.d: Replaces the understanding problem with a rule that first-time investors must start in an aggressive sector fund.

prompt: Keisha Grant, a nurse, asks about rolling her workplace retirement plan into an IRA. The representative recommends the rollover and describes the IRA's mutual funds. The representative never compares the plan's costs and services with the IRA. What is missing?

options.text: Nothing material, because describing the IRA fund menu completes a rollover recommendation.
The plan-versus-IRA comparison of costs and services, which a menu of IRA funds does not replace.
A tax-bracket worksheet, because rollover suitability is nothing beyond the customer's bracket.
A push to cash out the plan, because a thin rollover talk has to end in a taxable lump-sum distribution.

explanation: A rollover recommendation that never compares the workplace plan's costs and services with the IRA is incomplete. The representative should weigh what the plan already provides against the IRA before recommending the move. Describing the IRA fund menu is not that comparison. The analysis does not depend on inventing a tax bracket, and it does not default to cashing the plan out.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a description of the IRA fund menu as a complete rollover recommendation and skips the plan comparison.
distractorExplanations.c: Reduces rollover suitability to a tax-bracket worksheet and ignores costs and services.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns an incomplete rollover discussion into a recommendation to take a lump-sum cash-out.

prompt: Gloria Nguyen says she wants income from the account. Her representative sells her a growth mutual fund and explains the choice by saying the fund has done well lately. Gloria's profile does not list a growth objective. Why does the recommendation fail?

options.text: It does not fail, because a fund that has done well can stand in for the income objective Gloria stated.
It is unsuitable only after a down quarter, because a recent gain is what makes a growth fund fit an income goal.
A recent hot streak does not make this growth fund the income choice Gloria said she wants from this account.
It fails because growth funds are prohibited from making distributions, which is a fund-accounting violation.

explanation: Gloria wants income, and the representative sold a growth fund because it has done well. Recent performance is not a customer-specific reason to ignore the income objective. A growth fund is not barred from ever making a distribution, but a performance story does not convert it into an income recommendation. The profile's objective, not the recent record, drives the match.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses a strong recent record as a substitute for the income objective Gloria stated.
distractorExplanations.b: Makes suitability turn on whether the last quarter was up and treats a gain as proof a growth fund fits an income need.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a ban on distributions from growth funds instead of identifying the objective mismatch.

prompt: Marco Silva's entire account is already one technology-sector mutual fund. His representative recommends a second technology-sector fund and calls the purchase diversification. Marco has no holdings outside technology. What does the new purchase do?

options.text: It diversifies Marco, because owning two mutual funds spreads risk more than owning one, whatever sector they cover.
It cures the concentration, because a second technology fund holds different companies and therefore a different risk.
It raises quantitative suitability, because a single added fund counts as an excessive trading pattern.
It deepens the technology concentration he already has, rather than spreading the account outside that sector.

explanation: The account is already entirely in one technology fund. Adding another technology fund increases concentration in the same sector. Different companies inside that sector do not diversify away the sector risk, and calling the purchase diversification does not change the exposure. Customer-specific suitability includes concentration. One added purchase is not, by itself, a quantitative-suitability problem about an excessive series.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats any second mutual fund as diversification even when both funds are technology sector funds.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses different companies inside the same sector with a reduction in sector concentration.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels one additional purchase as quantitative suitability, which looks at whether a series of recommendations is excessive.

prompt: Yara Singh is saving money she plans to use in two years for a house. A representative recommends a variable annuity and builds the pitch on long-term tax-deferred accumulation inside the contract. What is wrong with that story for this goal?

options.text: Two-year house money is not served by a variable-annuity pitch built on long-term tax-deferred accumulation.
Nothing is wrong, because tax-deferred accumulation fits any goal dated at least a year out.
A money-market subaccount makes the annuity suitable, because that option erases the contract's other tradeoffs for a house fund.
The pitch is fine unless the house fund sits below a dollar cutoff the representative is supposed to compute before declining it.

explanation: Money needed in two years for a house is a short-horizon, specific-use goal. A variable-annuity accumulation story assumes a longer period of tax-deferred compounding and brings contract features, including surrender charges, that do not fit cash the client plans to spend on that schedule. A money-market subaccount does not turn the contract into a house fund. No dollar cutoff has to be invented to see the mismatch.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats tax-deferred accumulation as suitable for any goal that is at least a year away.
distractorExplanations.c: Assumes a money-market subaccount removes the annuity's surrender and contract tradeoffs for money needed in two years.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a dollar cutoff the representative must calculate before rejecting the accumulation pitch.

prompt: A representative uses one model portfolio of the same mutual funds, in the same weights, for every retail client. A retiree who needs income and a young client saving for a distant goal both receive that model. The representative says the model has already been vetted, so individual profiles are unnecessary. What fails?

options.text: Nothing fails, because firm approval of a model makes that same mix suitable for every retail customer.
Reasonable-basis suitability, because customer-specific suitability stops applying once a model portfolio is used.
Customer-specific suitability is what fails, because one vetted model is not a profile for both of these clients.
The communications rule fails, because a model portfolio is advertising and not a suitability question for either client.

explanation: The same model portfolio for every client fails customer-specific suitability. Reasonable-basis work on the funds inside the model does not match the mix to a retiree who needs income or to a young client with a long horizon. Reasonable-basis, customer-specific, and quantitative suitability are the three suitability components, and this shortcut skips the customer-specific one. Firm approval of a list is not a profile.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats firm approval of a model as if that approval made one mix suitable for every retail customer.
distractorExplanations.b: Says customer-specific suitability drops out once a model is used, and assigns the failure to reasonable-basis suitability.
distractorExplanations.d: Recasts a one-size-fits-all model as a communications issue and removes it from suitability.

prompt: Under forward pricing, a mutual fund order is filled:

options.text: At the NAV calculated at the prior day's close
At the next NAV calculated after the order arrives
At the NAV in effect when the client signs the form
At the average NAV over the previous five trading days

explanation: Rule 22c-1 requires forward pricing: purchase and redemption orders are priced at the next net asset value computed after the fund or its agent receives the order, usually at the 4 p.m. ET close.

distractorExplanations.a: Using a prior NAV is backward pricing, which the 1940 Act rules prohibit.
distractorExplanations.c: Signing a form does not set the price; receipt of the order does.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no averaging; each order gets the next computed NAV.
