prompt: Nora Pell prepares a public Instagram post urging followers to buy shares of the Northbridge Growth Fund. What must the firm do before that post is used?

options.text: Have a principal approve the post before it is used, because a public promotion of one fund is a retail communication.
Treat the post as correspondence that needs no advance approval, because each follower views it alone rather than as one audience.
Publish the post now and have a principal review it only if someone comments, because approval starts after a reply.
Send the post to the fund custodian for sign-off and skip the member firm's principal, because the custodian clears public fund posts.

explanation: Under FINRA Rule 2210, a communication available to more than 25 retail investors within 30 calendar days is a retail communication. A public post that promotes a specific mutual fund meets that test, so a registered principal must approve it before it is used.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a public post with correspondence. Correspondence is a message to 25 or fewer retail investors, not a post open to the public.
distractorExplanations.c: Mistimes the approval. The initial promotional post is static retail content and must be approved before first use, not after comments arrive.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns approval to the wrong party. The member firm that is publishing the retail communication must obtain its own principal's approval.

prompt: Malik Chen texts one existing client about the bond fund already held in that client's own account. How should the firm classify the text?

options.text: As a retail campaign that needs the same pre-use principal approval as a mailing to the firm's entire client list, because the text names a fund.
As correspondence about that one client's own holding, which the firm still supervises and which is not a retail campaign.
As an institutional communication, because an existing shareholder is treated as an institution once the fund is in the account.
As outside the communication rules, because a text message is not a written or electronic communication to a retail customer.

explanation: Correspondence is a written or electronic message sent to 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. One text to one existing client about that client's own fund is correspondence. It is still supervised, but it is not a retail campaign.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns every fund mention into a retail campaign. Naming the fund does not change a one-client text into a communication to more than 25 retail investors.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels the audience. An individual client who owns a fund is still a retail investor, not an institutional investor.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops the channel out of the rule. A text is an electronic communication and is covered; the audience size is what makes it correspondence.

prompt: A municipal-bond fund deck is emailed only to bank trust departments and registered investment advisers. The firm has no reason to believe those recipients will forward it to retail clients. What is the deck?

options.text: A retail communication, because each adviser serves households and those households are counted as if the firm had emailed them the deck directly.
Correspondence, because a PDF is reviewed after it goes out and the format, not the audience, sets the category.
An institutional communication, because the deck goes to banks and advisers rather than to retail investors.
A prospectus substitute, because any deck that names one municipal-bond fund replaces the prospectus for every recipient.

explanation: An institutional communication is distributed only to institutional investors. Banks and registered investment advisers are institutional investors. With no reason to believe the deck will be forwarded to retail clients, it remains an institutional communication rather than a retail piece.

distractorExplanations.a: Counts the institutions' underlying clients as the firm's audience. The category follows who receives the firm's communication, and here that audience is institutional.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the file format instead of the audience. A PDF sent only to institutional investors is an institutional communication, not correspondence.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a sales deck with prospectus delivery. Naming the fund in an institutional deck does not turn the deck into the statutory prospectus.

prompt: The firm drafts a retail brochure for the Harbor Deferred Variable Annuity by copying its equity-fund advertisement and changing the product name. What content treatment does this piece still need?

options.text: None beyond the equity-fund template, because a variable-annuity brochure is reviewed as an ordinary mutual-fund advertisement once the product name is swapped.
Language that calls the contract a mutual fund, so readers are not asked to distinguish a separate account from fund shares.
A required cooling-off period before any retail reader sees it, in place of product-specific variable-annuity disclosures.
Identification as a deferred variable annuity, not as a mutual fund, and a statement that contract value can fluctuate.

explanation: A retail communication about a deferred variable annuity must identify the contract as a variable annuity and must not describe it as an ordinary mutual fund. It also has to make clear that the contract value fluctuates with the separate account and can decline. Copying a generic fund advertisement leaves those points out. A principal still approves the retail piece before use.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the annuity brochure as a mutual-fund ad with a new title. The variable contract needs its own product identification and fluctuation disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Creates the misdescription the rule forbids. The piece must not present the deferred variable annuity as a mutual fund.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a cooling-off period in place of the content standard. The extra requirement is what the brochure says about the annuity, not a waiting period.

prompt: A retail magazine advertisement for the Cedar Equity Fund shows a five-star ranking and no other information about that ranking. What does the ranking rule require before the ad is used?

options.text: Disclose the ranking entity, the category, how many funds were ranked, the period covered, and the criteria used.
Leave the stars as they are, because a widely recognized star count already communicates the category, the period, the size of the peer group, and the basis of the ranking.
Remove the stars unless FINRA itself issued the rating, because a retail fund ad may show only a ranking prepared by the regulator.
Move the stars into a footnote and leave the category, the period, and the ranking entity off the page.

explanation: A retail advertisement that uses an investment-company ranking or star rating must disclose the ranking entity, the category, the number of funds in that category, the time period, and the criteria the ranking used. Printing the stars alone does not meet that standard, and the ranking must not be presented without those facts.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the star count as a complete disclosure. Readers are not expected to infer the category, the period, the peer-group size, or the criteria from the stars.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigns the ranking to FINRA. FINRA does not rate funds, and a third-party ranking may be used when the required disclosures are present.
distractorExplanations.d: Hides the ranking elements instead of disclosing them. A footnote that still omits the category, the period, and the ranking entity fails the same rule.

prompt: Priya Shah prepares an invitation and a slide deck for an open seminar advertised to retail prospects. How should the firm treat that seminar package?

options.text: As correspondence, because a seminar is a live talk and the invitation and slides are not communications distributed to the retail prospects who were invited.
As a retail communication, so a principal must approve both the invitation and the slides before they are used.
As an institutional communication, because a person who registers for a seminar is acting as an institution for that event.
As material that needs no principal approval unless Priya reads every slide aloud from a script during the seminar.

explanation: The invitation and slide deck for an open seminar advertised to retail prospects are communications made available to retail investors. That package is a retail communication under FINRA Rule 2210, so a registered principal must approve it before it is used.

distractorExplanations.a: Separates the printed seminar materials from the event. The invitation and slides distributed to retail prospects are themselves retail communications.
distractorExplanations.c: Relabels retail prospects as institutions because they signed up. Registration does not make a retail audience institutional.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits the approval rule to a scripted reading. The retail materials need principal approval before use whether or not the representative reads them word for word.

prompt: A compound-growth illustration for a mutual fund is handed to a prospect as the balance the account will reach. How may that illustration be presented?

options.text: As the balance the client will have if the client stays invested, because a printed growth path is a commitment once the representative hands it over.
As a guarantee of the ending value, because firm letterhead converts a hypothetical path into a promised result the client can rely on.
As a clearly labeled illustration of a mathematical idea, and never as the ending balance the prospect's account will reach.
As a forecast the client should expect, with the hypothetical label removed so the page reads as the representative's projection of performance.

explanation: FINRA Rule 2210 bars a communication that predicts performance or hands a growth path over as the balance the account will reach. A compound-growth figure may illustrate a mathematical idea only when it is clearly labeled hypothetical and is not offered as that result.

distractorExplanations.a: Converts the illustration into a promised balance. Handing a client a growth path does not make that ending value a result the account will reach.
distractorExplanations.b: Turns a hypothetical into a guarantee. Letterhead does not change an illustration into a promise, and a mutual fund's future value cannot be guaranteed this way.
distractorExplanations.d: Removes the feature that keeps the illustration honest. Dropping the hypothetical label and calling the path a forecast is a prohibited projection.

prompt: A client phones Jordan Hale about a mutual-fund switch, then emails the same grievance the next morning. Jordan already apologized on the phone and marks the matter handled. What is still required?

options.text: Nothing further, because the phone apology closed the matter and the later email does not have to reach the complaint file.
A request that the client withdraw the email, so the phone apology remains the record of the mutual-fund switch.
A note in Jordan's personal notebook, with the firm's complaint file left out of the email the client already sent.
Keep the client's email in the firm's complaint file, because that written grievance is the complaint record.

explanation: A FINRA complaint record is a written grievance. The email is that writing, so it belongs in the firm's complaint file. The phone apology does not close the matter once the client has put the grievance in writing.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the phone apology as a waiver of the written grievance. The email is a complaint and still has to reach the firm's complaint file.
distractorExplanations.b: Asks the client to withdraw the email so the apology stands alone. Hiding the writing is the opposite of keeping the complaint on file.
distractorExplanations.c: Keeps the record personal. A notebook the firm never sees does not place the written grievance in the complaint file.

prompt: To persuade a hesitant client to buy the Oakmont Income Fund, a representative offers a weekend trip if the client signs the purchase form. How should that offer be treated?

options.text: As an improper inducement, because the weekend trip is offered on the condition that the client signs the form to buy the fund.
As permitted once the client asks for the trip in writing, because a written request turns the inducement into an ordinary customer order.
As permitted under the annual gift allowance, because a gift conditioned on a purchase is handled like a routine courtesy and does not need a separate look at why it was offered.
As permitted if the trip is delivered after the sale settles, because an inducement counts only when the gift changes hands before the trade ticket is entered.

explanation: A gift offered so the customer will buy a particular fund is an inducement tied to the sale. That purpose makes the gift improper. The conclusion does not depend on a dollar cap, on moving the gift until after settlement, or on relabeling it as a routine courtesy.

distractorExplanations.b: Relabels an inducement as an order. The client's written request for the trip does not make a purchase-conditioned gift proper.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies a gift-allowance idea to a sale inducement. A gift given to influence the purchase is improper because of its purpose, not because of where it sits against an allowance.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the same inducement to a later date. Delivering the trip after settlement does not remove the link between the gift and the fund sale.

prompt: Elena Voss, a registered representative, told her manager in the hallway that she wants to open a paid weekend bookkeeping service for local shops while she remains with her member firm. What must she still do before that service starts?

options.text: Start the service and tell the firm if a bookkeeping client later complains about her securities work.
Give the member firm prior written notice of the paid bookkeeping service before that work starts.
Treat the hallway comment as enough, because a side business kept off the firm's letterhead does not need written notice.
Begin the work now and mention it at the next registration-renewal cycle, because advance notice applies when the outside job sells the same products as the firm.

explanation: FINRA Rule 3270 requires a registered person to give the member firm prior written notice before starting an outside business activity for which she is paid or expects to be paid. A hallway conversation is not that writing. The firm may then restrict or prohibit the activity. Paid bookkeeping is covered, and notice after the work has already started does not satisfy the rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Delays notice until a complaint. The rule requires written notice before the paid activity begins, not after a problem shows up.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a side business kept off the firm's letterhead as private. Paid bookkeeping still needs prior written notice to the firm, whether or not she uses the firm's name.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a later renewal disclosure for prior notice. She cannot start the business and wait for the next cycle to tell the firm.

prompt: A college friend asks Chris Adelman to introduce investors to a private placement and offers Chris a selling commission. Chris would do the work away from his firm. What does the private-securities rule require?

options.text: Nothing from the firm, because helping a friend place securities for a commission is a personal favor rather than a transaction the member has to approve.
A courtesy notice after the interests have been sold, because approval is required when the representative's own firm is the issuer of the private placement.
The firm's written approval before Chris participates, because the selling commission pays him for a securities deal away from the firm.
The outside-business notice, with no separate approval, because a compensated placement away from the firm is not a private securities transaction.

explanation: FINRA Rule 3280 requires prior written notice of a private securities transaction away from the firm. When the representative will receive selling compensation, the firm must approve the transaction in writing before he participates. If the firm approves, the transaction is recorded on the firm's books. A commission for helping a friend is selling compensation, not a personal favor.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls compensated selling away a personal favor. A private placement sold for a commission is a private securities transaction and needs the firm's written approval.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the timing and the trigger. Notice and the firm's approval have to come before he participates, and the friend's deal does not have to be issued by Chris's firm.
distractorExplanations.d: Stops at outside-business notice. A compensated securities transaction away from the firm is a private securities transaction and needs written approval, not notice alone.

prompt: A customer tells Amy Cho, by phone, to choose the mutual funds and the dollar amounts in the account from now on. What has to be in place before Amy uses that authority?

options.text: Nothing further, because a spoken instruction is written authorization when the customer and the representative already know each other and the first trades can document the phone call.
Only Amy's good-faith reading of the call, because choosing the fund and the amount is time-and-price discretion and that limited authority needs no prior writing.
A signed discretionary form sometime after the first purchases, because the writing can catch up once the opening trades have been placed.
The customer's prior written authorization to choose the funds and the amounts, plus the firm's written acceptance, in place before any trade.

explanation: Authority to choose the security and the amount is discretion over the account. The customer must give prior written authorization, and the firm must accept the account in writing, before the representative exercises that authority. A phone call is not the writing. Time-and-price discretion is narrower: it does not let the representative pick the fund or the size.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a phone call as prior written authorization. Familiarity with the customer does not convert a spoken grant of discretion into the required writing.
distractorExplanations.b: Misnames the authority. Time-and-price discretion applies only after the customer has chosen the security and the amount, which this customer has not done.
distractorExplanations.c: Allows the trades to come first. The written authorization and the firm's acceptance must already be in place before Amy chooses funds and amounts.

prompt: Luis Ortega's sister, a representative at another broker-dealer, asks Luis for a client's fund holdings and account balance so she can solicit that client. What does Regulation S-P require Luis to do?

options.text: Refuse to hand his sister the holdings and the balance, because those facts are nonpublic personal information she has no right to use.
Send the holdings and the balance but withhold the account number, because a list of positions without the account number is public information his sister may use.
Share the holdings and the balance if his sister promises to keep them inside her firm, because Regulation S-P treats a family member at another broker-dealer as an affiliate.
Share the information after the sister sells the client a fund, because a completed sale at the other firm cures the disclosure of the holdings and the balance.

explanation: Regulation S-P protects a customer's nonpublic personal information, including fund holdings and account balances. Luis may not hand that information to his sister at another firm so she can solicit the client. The other firm is not an affiliate, and a family relationship is not an exception that permits the disclosure.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats holdings and balances as public once the account number is removed. Those details are still nonpublic personal information and cannot be sent for the sister's solicitation.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an affiliate exception for family. A sibling who works at another broker-dealer is a nonaffiliated third party, and a promise to keep the file quiet does not authorize the disclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: Puts the disclosure on the wrong side of the sale. A later purchase at the sister's firm does not excuse sharing the client's nonpublic information.

prompt: A walk-in customer who wants to open a mutual-fund account gives only a first name and promises to bring a driver's license to a later appointment. What is the status of the customer identification program?

options.text: It is satisfied, because the program is complete once the customer promises to bring a license later and the account can be opened on a first name in the meantime.
It is not satisfied, because a first name and a promise of a later license leave out the information the program requires.
It is satisfied, because a first name can be recorded as the taxpayer identification number until the license arrives at the later appointment.
It does not apply, because the identification program covers margin and options accounts and not an account used only to buy mutual funds.

explanation: The customer identification program requires the customer's name, date of birth, residential or business address, and an identification number, and the firm must verify the customer's identity. A first name plus a promise to bring a license later does not collect those facts and does not complete the program.

distractorExplanations.a: Accepts a promise in place of the required information. The program is not complete when the firm has only a first name and a statement that identification will come later.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes a given name for the identification number. A first name is not a taxpayer identification number and does not finish the identifying information.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits the program to margin and options. A mutual-fund account at a broker-dealer is still an account the customer identification program covers.

prompt: On a first call, Samir Patel recommends a sector fund and says the new-account profile can be completed after the trade is placed. When do the know-your-customer essential facts have to be known?

options.text: After the trade, because the essential facts are a file that documents a recommendation the representative has already made to the customer.
Only if the customer asks for a questionnaire, because essential facts are optional when the caller sounds comfortable choosing a sector fund.
Before the sector-fund recommendation, because the essential facts about this customer have to be known before that recommendation.
They can be replaced by the fund's investment objective, because the essential facts are facts about the security rather than facts about the customer.

explanation: FINRA's know-your-customer rule requires the firm to know the essential facts about the customer so the account can be serviced and the recommendation can be judged. Those facts come before the recommendation. Finishing the profile after the sector-fund trade reverses that order.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the profile as an after-the-fact record. Essential facts are gathered so the representative can recommend, not so the file can catch up after the trade.
distractorExplanations.b: Makes the profile optional for a confident caller. The customer's tone on the phone does not excuse knowing the essential facts before the recommendation.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps the fund's objective for the customer's facts. The essential facts are about the customer, including who holds authority and how the account is to be served.

prompt: Shares of the Northwind Equity Fund are sold to a client today. The representative plans to mail the prospectus with next month's account statement. When must the client receive the prospectus?

options.text: With next month's account statement, because delivery any time before that statement is mailed counts as delivery at the sale of the fund.
If the client requests one, because a mutual-fund purchase can be completed from the confirmation without a prospectus unless the client asks.
Not in this sale, if the client instead receives the statement of additional information, because that statement is the document required at or before the sale.
At or before the client buys the Northwind shares, rather than with the account statement mailed the following month.

explanation: The client must receive the fund's prospectus at or before the sale. Mailing it with the next monthly account statement delivers it after the sale and does not meet that timing. The statement of additional information is available on request; it does not replace the prospectus.

distractorExplanations.a: Moves delivery to the next statement cycle. A prospectus that arrives with the following month's statement comes after the sale.
distractorExplanations.b: Makes prospectus delivery optional. The representative cannot wait for the client to request the prospectus before handing it over on a fund sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps in the statement of additional information. That statement supplements the prospectus and is not a substitute for delivery at or before the sale.

prompt: A representative gives a client the summary prospectus for a load fund and says the sales charge can be left out of the discussion because the short form replaced the fee table. What is the right treatment of the sales charge?

options.text: The sales charge must still be disclosed, because the summary prospectus keeps the fee table and does not hide the charge.
The sales charge can be omitted from the conversation, because the summary prospectus replaces the fee table and the client must request costs in a separate document.
The fund can be described as having no sales charge whenever the summary prospectus is the document handed to the client.
The statutory prospectus must be withheld, because delivery of the summary prospectus ends the client's right to the fuller prospectus and its fee table.

explanation: A summary prospectus still includes the fee table, and the sales charge is part of that table. Using the summary prospectus does not let the representative conceal the charge or describe the fund as having none. The statutory prospectus remains available to the client.

distractorExplanations.b: Claims the short form deleted the fee table. The summary prospectus contains the fee information, and the representative may not skip the sales charge because the document is shorter.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a no-load status the document does not support. Handing over a summary prospectus does not erase a sales charge the fee table shows.
distractorExplanations.d: Cancels a document the client can still get. The summary prospectus does not end the right to the statutory prospectus, and neither version is a reason to hide the charge.

prompt: A retail banner for the Pine Street Bond Fund states in large type that the fund is no risk. How should the firm treat that banner?

options.text: Use it, because a bond fund returns principal at maturity and a retail banner may describe that kind of fund as having no risk to the investor who holds the shares.
Do not use that banner in this form, because telling a retail reader that the bond fund has no risk is a misleading claim.
Use it if a footnote calls the phrase a slogan, because a headline claim of no risk is fair when the footnote says the words are promotional.
Use it on the public website after the file notes that the audience was meant to be institutional, because the internal note changes the claim.

explanation: A mutual fund, including a bond fund, can lose value. FINRA Rule 2210 requires retail communications to be fair, balanced, and not misleading. A banner that calls the fund no risk fails that standard and cannot be used in that form.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a bond fund as risk-free. Bond prices move with interest rates and credit, and fund shares are not a promise that the investor cannot lose money.
distractorExplanations.c: Tries to cure the headline with a slogan label. Calling the claim a slogan does not make a no-risk statement about a mutual fund fair or balanced.
distractorExplanations.d: Relies on an internal note while the banner is on a public retail site. A file comment does not convert a misleading retail claim into a permitted one.

prompt: After hours, Devon Clark drafts a public Facebook post on his personal profile naming his firm's small-cap fund and urging people to buy it. He plans to tell a principal in the morning. When does principal approval have to happen?

options.text: The next morning is soon enough, because a personal profile is outside the retail-communication rules until a client comments, and a screenshot after publication satisfies the approval step.
Approval is unnecessary, because a post written after hours about a fund the firm already sells is correspondence no matter how public the profile is.
Before the post goes up on the personal profile, because that profile does not postpone principal approval of a public fund promotion.
Only at the fund company, because the member firm's principal does not review a representative's post when the post names a specific fund.

explanation: A representative's public post promoting a fund is a firm communication even when it is published from a personal profile. A public promotional post is a retail communication, and a principal must approve it before it is used. Posting first and telling a principal the next morning misses that timing.

distractorExplanations.a: Moves approval until after publication and treats the personal profile as exempt. The profile does not take a public fund promotion outside the rule, and approval has to come before the post is used.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls a public post correspondence because of the hour it was written. Audience, not the time of night, decides the category, and this post is public.
distractorExplanations.d: Sends the review to the fund company. The member firm must approve its associated person's retail communication before use.

prompt: Holly Ng sends the same reply to 20 existing retail clients who each asked about the balanced fund already held in that client's account. All 20 emails go out within two weeks. How may the firm classify them?

options.text: As an institutional communication, because existing clients become institutions for any email that discusses a fund they already own.
As prospectus delivery, because emails that mention the balanced fund stand in for the prospectus of that fund.
As a retail communication that needs pre-use principal approval, because the reply went to 20 people and any group larger than one retail client is a retail campaign.
As correspondence the firm still supervises, because 20 retail clients in two weeks is not more than 25.

explanation: Correspondence is a written or electronic communication sent to 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. Twenty retail clients in two weeks stays on that side of the line, so the firm may classify the replies as correspondence and still supervise them. Sending the same reply to more than one client, or naming the fund, does not by itself make a retail campaign.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns existing retail clients into institutions. Owning the fund does not change their status, and these 20 recipients are still retail investors.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a client-service email with prospectus delivery. Mentioning the balanced fund does not make the email the prospectus of that fund.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats any group larger than one as a retail campaign. The retail line is more than 25 retail investors in 30 calendar days, and 20 clients in two weeks is still correspondence.

prompt: Retail seminar slides say a third-party service ranked the firm's international fund first. The slides give no date, no ranking entity, and no category. What must the retail material include?

options.text: The date or period of the ranking, the ranking entity, the category, and the other disclosures that rule requires.
Nothing more, because an undated claim that the fund ranked first remains usable for as long as the representative remembers that the ranking was once true.
No third-party ranking at all, because retail material may cite a ranking only when the member firm created the ranking itself.
The ranking spoken aloud with no source and no date, as long as the undated line is removed from the slides the audience can read.

explanation: A third-party ranking used in retail material has to be current, and the material has to disclose the date or time period of the ranking, the ranking entity, the category, the number of funds ranked, and the criteria. An undated line that a fund ranked first does not meet that standard.

distractorExplanations.b: Keeps a stale or undated ranking in circulation on the representative's memory. The rule requires the date or period and the other ranking disclosures, not a recollection that the rank was once true.
distractorExplanations.c: Bans third-party rankings. An independent ranking may be used in retail material when it is current and the required disclosures, including the date or period, are present.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the same omission into the spoken remarks. Taking the line off the slide and saying it without a source or a date still fails the disclosure requirement.

prompt: During a recommendation, a representative tells a client that the Larkspur Growth Fund is appropriate because FINRA approved the fund. What must the representative do with that statement?

options.text: Leave it unchanged, because a principal's review of the firm's sales material means FINRA has approved the merits of the fund being recommended.
Withdraw the statement and correct the client, because FINRA does not approve or endorse the fund being recommended.
Limit it to existing customers, because the prohibition on saying FINRA approved a fund applies only while the listener is still a prospect.
Keep the claim and add that the firm is a FINRA member, because stating membership is the same thing as stating that FINRA approved the fund's merits.

explanation: FINRA does not approve or endorse a mutual fund, and a representative must not say that it does. A principal's review of an advertisement, and the firm's FINRA membership, are not a regulator's approval of the fund. The statement has to be withdrawn and corrected.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a principal's review with FINRA approval. The firm's approval of its own material is not a statement that FINRA approved the fund.
distractorExplanations.c: Limits the prohibition to prospects. The representative cannot tell an existing customer that FINRA approved the fund either.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats membership as product approval. The firm may identify itself as a FINRA member, but that sentence does not mean FINRA approved the fund.

prompt: Over two days, a customer buys the same money-market fund with currency each time just below the amount that would trigger a large-cash report. The representative notices the pattern. What should the representative do?

options.text: Tell the customer to bring the currency in one larger deposit so the tickets sit over the reporting line, and then complete the purchases without calling a supervisor.
Ignore the pattern, because each ticket was below the large-cash line and a red flag exists only when a single deposit crosses that line.
Escalate the pattern to supervision, and do not tell the customer that a suspicious-activity report is being considered.
Call the customer, explain that a suspicious-activity report is being considered, and wait for the customer's explanation before supervision is told.

explanation: Repeated currency purchases kept just below a large-cash reporting amount are a red flag for structuring. The representative must escalate the pattern to supervision and must not coach the customer or reveal that a suspicious-activity report is being considered. The representative does not clear the flag alone.

distractorExplanations.a: Coaches the customer through the reporting line and cuts supervision out. Helping the customer restructure the cash, and staying silent inside the firm, compounds the red flag.
distractorExplanations.b: Looks at each ticket in isolation. Splitting cash so that every purchase stays under the reporting amount is itself the pattern supervision needs to see.
distractorExplanations.d: Tips off the customer and delays the escalation. The representative must not tell the customer that a suspicious-activity report is under consideration.

prompt: Before the Harbor Index Fund order is entered, the client calls and asks the representative to change the account designation to a cousin's name. The request is verbal. What does that change require?

options.text: That phone call, because the purchaser's verbal instruction is the firm's documentation and a principal does not have to approve a change of account name.
An automatic refusal, because an account designation is locked to the new-account form and cannot be changed before the order is entered.
A text message to the cousin, because telling the proposed owner is the approval the firm needs before the designation is changed.
Written approval by a principal who has been given the essential facts, with those facts documented before the designation changes.

explanation: A change of account name or designation has to be approved in writing by a principal who has been told the essential facts, and those facts have to be documented before the change. A verbal request is not that approval and is not the firm's record.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the phone call as the firm record. A verbal request does not replace the principal's written approval or the documented essential facts.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the designation as locked to the new-account form. It can be changed before the order is entered when a principal approves the change and the facts are documented.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes a text to the cousin for the firm's approval. Notice to the proposed owner is not the principal's written authorization or the required record.

prompt: A representative recommends a target-date fund to a new retail customer and offers Form CRS only after the shares have been bought, as a souvenir of the sale. When must Form CRS be delivered?

options.text: Before or at the time of the target-date recommendation, not after the shares have been bought as a souvenir.
If the customer later asks for a relationship summary, because a recommendation does not itself start the duty to deliver Form CRS.
Not in this sale, because the target-date fund prospectus replaces Form CRS for a retail customer who is buying a mutual fund.
At the next annual account review, because a recommendation of a target-date fund does not start the Form CRS delivery timing for a new retail customer.

explanation: A broker-dealer must deliver Form CRS to a retail customer before or at the time of a recommendation of a securities transaction or investment strategy. Handing it over after the shares have been purchased, as a souvenir, misses that timing. The fund prospectus does not take the place of Form CRS.

distractorExplanations.b: Waits for the customer to ask. Delivery is required before or at the recommendation, not only when the customer requests a relationship summary afterward.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the prospectus for Form CRS. The prospectus discloses the fund; Form CRS discloses the relationship, and both jobs are required on their own timing.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays delivery until an annual review. The recommendation itself is a delivery trigger, so the form is already late if it arrives only at the next review.

prompt: Under a networking arrangement, a representative sits at a desk in a bank lobby and describes a mutual fund to walk-in customers. Which disclosure does that setting still require?

options.text: No insurance disclosure, because a networking arrangement on bank premises makes the mutual fund a deposit obligation of the bank.
That the fund is not a bank deposit, is not FDIC insured, is not guaranteed by the bank, and can lose value.
That FDIC insurance covers the mutual fund up to the bank's deposit limit, because the conversation happens inside the lobby next to the teller line and the customer already banks there.
That the bank guarantees the fund, because the bank allowed the representative to use a desk in the lobby for securities conversations.

explanation: On a bank premises under a networking arrangement, communications about securities must make clear that the investment is not a deposit or other obligation of the bank, is not FDIC insured, is not guaranteed by the bank, and is subject to investment risk, including possible loss of principal. The lobby location does not transfer deposit insurance to the fund.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the networking location as if it converted the fund into a bank deposit. The arrangement is a reason the non-deposit disclosure is required, not a reason to skip it.
distractorExplanations.c: Extends the bank's FDIC insurance to the fund. Mutual-fund shares sold at the desk are not insured deposits, even when the customer also holds a bank account.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a bank guarantee from the use of the desk. Permission to sit in the lobby does not make the bank a guarantor of the fund.

prompt: A newspaper ad describes mutual funds in general and names no particular fund. A representative then treats that ad as the prospectus for a sale of the Riverside Growth Fund. What is the right relationship between the ad and the sale?

options.text: The newspaper ad is the prospectus for whichever fund the client buys next, because a general description of mutual funds replaces the prospectus of the specific fund being sold.
The firm must stop generic ads, because an advertisement that does not name a fund is not allowed and cannot sit beside a real fund sale.
The generic newspaper ad is not an offer of the Riverside fund, so that fund's prospectus is still due at or before the sale.
The ad can be filed as the statement of additional information for the Riverside fund, which completes delivery for the sale without the prospectus.

explanation: Generic advertising that does not name a specific security describes mutual funds as a product type. It is not a prospectus and it is not an offer of one named fund. A sale of the Riverside Growth Fund still requires that fund's prospectus at or before the sale.

distractorExplanations.a: Promotes the generic ad into the prospectus of a named fund. A piece that names no fund does not satisfy prospectus delivery for the Riverside Growth Fund.
distractorExplanations.b: Bans generic advertising. An ad that does not name a specific fund is permitted generic advertising; it is simply not the prospectus offer of one fund.
distractorExplanations.d: Files the ad as the statement of additional information. That statement does not replace the prospectus, and a generic newspaper ad is neither document.

prompt: A client posts, on the Instagram profile Nina Boyd uses with her clients, that Nina's fund picks doubled the client's account. Nina leaves the post up. What is that testimonial from the firm's point of view?

options.text: A testimonial the firm still has to supervise, including whether that performance claim may stay on the profile.
Outside the firm's supervision, because the client wrote the sentence and a compliment on that profile is not the member's communication.
Safe to leave up once Nina comments that doubling is a typical result, because her agreement makes a performance post fair without firm review.
Outside the firm's communications, because Nina did not type the sentence and a client's own words are never attributed to the representative who leaves them posted.

explanation: The profile is one Nina uses with her clients, and she left a client's claim that an account doubled on it. That performance statement is a communication the firm has to supervise, including whether it may stay and what disclosures it needs. The duty does not disappear because Nina did not type the sentence.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the profile as exempt because the client wrote the words. She uses the profile with clients and left a performance claim up, so the firm still has to supervise it.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses the representative's own comment as a substitute for supervision. Agreeing that the result is typical does not make an unsupervised performance testimonial compliant.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits the rule to sentences the representative typed. Adopting a client's testimonial by leaving it up still makes it a communication the firm must supervise.

prompt: A long-time customer offers to lend Owen Briggs money for a home repair. Owen wants to sign a private IOU and keep the loan off the firm's books. How must borrowing from a customer be handled?

options.text: As a private loan the firm does not see, because the customer's offer and the representative's signature are the whole arrangement the borrowing rule requires.
As a handshake loan, because a no-interest home-repair loan can stay between them and the firm steps in if the customer charges interest.
Under the firm's written procedures and the prior approval those procedures require, rather than through a private IOU.
By taking the money and staying silent, because a home-repair loan from a customer is allowed on its own and the firm is told if the representative defaults.

explanation: A representative may not borrow from a customer as a private arrangement the firm never hears about. FINRA's borrowing rule permits a loan only when the firm's written procedures allow the arrangement and the representative obtains the prior approval those procedures require. An IOU kept off the firm's books fails that rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats mutual agreement as a substitute for the firm. The customer's willingness to lend does not make a side loan proper when the firm is never told.
distractorExplanations.b: Limits the writing to interest-bearing loans. The firm has to be in the arrangement whether or not the customer charges interest, and a handshake is not the firm's procedure.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes a home-repair purpose creates an automatic permission. The purpose of the loan does not excuse silence, and default is not the event that first brings the firm in.

prompt: A customer proposes that Renee Holt take half of any gains in the customer's mutual-fund account. They shake hands on the split. What does sharing in those profits require?

options.text: The handshake, because an oral percentage agreed by the customer and the representative is the firm's authorization to share in the account.
A text from the customer stating the percentage, because profit sharing can rest on that message and the firm's writing is for arrangements that also split losses.
The firm's and the customer's prior written authorizations before any split of the gains, which the handshake does not provide.
Notice to the firm at year-end, after half of the gains have already been moved to Renee, because the writing can follow the first profitable period.

explanation: Sharing in the profits or losses of a customer's account requires the member firm's prior written authorization and the customer's prior written authorization. The representative's share must also be proportional to the money each person contributed, unless the customer is the representative's immediate family. A handshake supplies none of those writings.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the handshake as the firm's authorization. An oral split between the customer and the representative is not the prior written authorization the firm must give.
distractorExplanations.b: Limits the firm's writing to loss-sharing and accepts a customer text in its place. Profit sharing needs the firm's prior written authorization whether or not losses are shared too.
distractorExplanations.d: Lets the split happen first. The firm's written authorization has to be in place before the representative shares in the gains, not after a year of taking half.

prompt: A SEP IRA is characterized by which funding rule?

options.text: Employees fund it through salary deferrals only
The employer funds it at the same rate for all
The employer may choose which staff to fund
Employee and employer contributions must match

explanation: A SEP IRA is funded only by the employer, which must contribute the same percentage of compensation for every eligible employee in any year it contributes.

distractorExplanations.a: SEP IRAs are funded by employer contributions, not employee deferrals.
distractorExplanations.c: SEP contributions must be the same percentage of pay for all eligible employees.
distractorExplanations.d: There are no employee contributions to match in a SEP.

prompt: Mara wants her traditional IRA moved from Harbor Trust directly to Northline Custody. The two custodians will move the assets, and Mara will never receive a check. How should the rep classify that move?

options.text: A trustee-to-trustee transfer, not a 60-day rollover
An indirect rollover that uses her one IRA-to-IRA rollover for the next 12 months
A taxable distribution caused by the change of custodian
A Roth conversion that is ordinary income this year

explanation: When one IRA custodian moves assets straight to another IRA custodian, and the owner never receives the money, the move is a trustee-to-trustee transfer. It is not a 60-day rollover, and it does not use the once-per-12-months limit that applies to IRA-to-IRA indirect rollovers.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a direct custodian-to-custodian transfer with an indirect rollover. Only a distribution the owner receives and redeposits counts toward the one-rollover limit.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a change of IRA custodian as a distribution. Assets that stay inside an IRA through a direct transfer are not taxed as a distribution.
distractorExplanations.d: Mislabels a traditional-to-traditional custodian change as a Roth conversion. No conversion income arises from the transfer.

prompt: In March, Luis received a check from one traditional IRA and deposited it into a second traditional IRA within 60 days. In October he wants another check payable to himself, to deposit into a third IRA within 60 days. What should the rep tell him?

options.text: He may take the October check because the one-rollover limit starts over for every IRA he owns
That second indirect rollover is not allowed in this 12-month period
The October check is a trustee-to-trustee transfer
Both checks are taxable even if redeposited on time

explanation: An IRA owner may complete only one IRA-to-IRA indirect rollover in any 12-month period, counting all of the owner's IRAs together. Luis already used that rollover in March, so a second check payable to him in October cannot be rolled the same way. A trustee-to-trustee transfer would have been different: it is not an indirect rollover and does not use that once-per-12-months limit.

distractorExplanations.a: Splits the one-rollover rule by account. The 12-month limit applies across the owner's IRAs, not once per IRA.
distractorExplanations.c: Misnames a check payable to Luis. A trustee-to-trustee transfer moves assets between custodians and is not paid to the owner.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a timely indirect rollover as taxable. The March rollover can be tax-free; the problem is that a second one inside 12 months is not allowed.

prompt: Priya, age 46, will move pre-tax dollars from her traditional IRA into a Roth IRA this year. The custodian will send the full amount to the Roth. A coworker says that because she is under 59½, the 10% additional tax applies to the conversion on top of income tax. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Income tax waits until a Roth withdrawal, and the 10% additional tax applies now
The conversion is tax-free because the dollars land in a Roth IRA
The pre-tax amount is ordinary income this year and draws no 10% tax
She can elect last year's lower bracket so this conversion adds nothing she owes

explanation: Pre-tax money moved from a traditional IRA into a Roth IRA is ordinary income in the year of the conversion. When the custodian sends the full amount to the Roth, the conversion itself is not subject to the 10% additional tax, even though Priya is 46. That additional tax can still apply to money she keeps and does not convert. The income is not postponed until a later Roth withdrawal, the Roth label does not make pre-tax dollars tax-free, and she cannot elect a prior year's bracket to erase this year's tax.

distractorExplanations.a: Splits the result the wrong way. The pre-tax amount is income this year, and a full conversion is not itself subject to the 10% additional tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats the Roth destination as an exemption. Pre-tax dollars are still ordinary income in the conversion year.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a prior-year bracket she can elect. The converted pre-tax amount is income on this year's return.

prompt: Andre left his job. The 401(k) will mail an eligible-rollover check payable to Andre, and he plans to deposit it into an IRA within 60 days. How is withholding handled on that check?

options.text: Nothing is withheld if he promises to redeposit the full check in an IRA within 60 days
The plan withholds 10% because that is the early-distribution rate
Withholding is taken only when Andre asks the plan to take tax out
The plan withholds 20% because this eligible rollover is paid to Andre

explanation: An eligible rollover distribution paid to the participant is subject to 20% mandatory withholding, even if he intends to complete a 60-day rollover. A direct rollover paid to the receiving IRA avoids that withholding. If Andre rolls only the cash he receives, the 20% that was withheld is a taxable distribution unless he replaces it from other money and rolls the full taxable amount within 60 days.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats an intended 60-day rollover as a waiver of withholding. The plan still withholds 20% when the eligible rollover is paid to Andre.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the 10% additional early-distribution tax with withholding. The mandatory withholding rate on this check is 20%.
distractorExplanations.c: Makes the 20% withholding optional. On an eligible rollover paid to the person, the withholding is mandatory.

prompt: Denise changed employers in June. Her former employer's 401(k) still holds her vested balance, and that plan lets terminated participants leave money in the plan. She asks whether she must roll it over. What is accurate?

options.text: She may leave the balance in the old plan; the job change does not force a rollover
Leaving the vested balance in the old plan taxes the whole amount this year, so a 60-day IRA move is required
The job change itself moves the old balance into the new employer's plan before the next payroll
A former employee cannot keep a 401(k) balance, so the plan pays the vested amount out in cash

explanation: Changing jobs does not by itself require a rollover. When the former employer's plan permits a terminated participant to leave the vested balance in the plan, leaving it there is a real choice. An IRA rollover, a rollover to a new employer's plan, or a cash distribution are alternatives, not obligations created by the job change.

distractorExplanations.b: Turns an optional rollover into a tax bill and a deadline. Leaving the balance in a plan that allows it is not a distribution, and she does not have to move it to an IRA.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the job change as an automatic transfer into the new employer's plan. Separation does not, by itself, move the old balance.
distractorExplanations.d: Claims a former employee must be cashed out. The plan in these facts allows the vested balance to stay, so a cash-out is not required.

prompt: Owen is self-employed and has no job with a school or a nonprofit. He asks the rep to open a 403(b) for him the same way he would open an IRA. What is the right response?

options.text: Any worker may open a 403(b) the same way he opens an IRA
A 403(b) is for certain school and nonprofit employees, not an IRA he opens alone
He can open it at a fund company on his own because a 403(b) is only a traditional IRA with a different label
A 403(b) is a governmental 457 plan under another code section

explanation: A 403(b) is an employer plan for employees of public schools and certain tax-exempt organizations, and some ministers can be covered as well. It is not an IRA that a worker opens on his own. Owen is self-employed and has no school or tax-exempt employer in these facts, so he cannot open a 403(b) the way he opens an IRA.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a 403(b) as a personal IRA available to any worker. Eligibility is tied to the employer, not to a desire for tax-deferred savings.
distractorExplanations.c: Renames a traditional IRA as a 403(b). The two are different vehicles, and a fund company cannot open a 403(b) for him without an eligible employer.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps a 403(b) for a 457 plan. A 457 is a separate deferred-compensation plan, not the label for a 403(b).

prompt: A city clerk tells the rep that her 457 plan is a 401(k) with a different name, so every 401(k) distribution rule applies unchanged. How should the rep classify the 457?

options.text: A traditional IRA the city opened in her name
A 403(b) reserved for public-school teachers
A separate employer plan, not a 401(k) under another name
A 401(k) in every respect, so the 457 label changes nothing about loans, rollovers, or distributions

explanation: A 457 plan is its own type of employer deferred-compensation plan. It is not a traditional IRA, not a 403(b), and not a 401(k) under another name. Distribution rules do not copy over unchanged. A distribution from a governmental 457(b) is generally not subject to the 10% additional tax, except on amounts rolled in from a plan or IRA that is subject to that tax. A 401(k) distribution can still draw the 10% additional tax before age 59½ when no exception applies.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns an employer 457 into a personal traditional IRA. The city plan is not an IRA the clerk owns outside the employer arrangement.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns the account to the 403(b) rules used for school and nonprofit employees. A 457 is a different plan type.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the 457 label as cosmetic. It is a separate plan, so 401(k) distribution rules do not automatically govern it.

prompt: Helen deferred part of her salary under her company's nonqualified deferred compensation agreement. She asks the rep to roll that unpaid promise into an IRA the way a qualified-plan payout rolls. What is she holding?

options.text: An ERISA qualified plan she can roll into an IRA on the same terms as a 401(k) payout
A traditional IRA the company already funded in her name
A Roth IRA, so the deferred salary is already after-tax
An unfunded promise of later pay, not an IRA or a qualified plan

explanation: Nonqualified deferred compensation is an employer's unfunded promise to pay later. It is not an IRA, and it is not an ERISA qualified plan such as a 401(k). The unpaid deferral is not an eligible rollover distribution that she can move into an IRA the way a qualified-plan payout can be rolled.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives the deferral qualified-plan rollover treatment. Nonqualified deferred compensation is outside the qualified-plan rollover rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Assumes the employer already funded a traditional IRA. The arrangement is a promise to pay, not an IRA contribution.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls the deferral a Roth IRA. Deferred salary under a nonqualified agreement is not a Roth contribution.

prompt: Chris, age 48, takes a cash distribution from his traditional IRA and spends it. A colleague says the 10% additional tax applies to every IRA distribution taken before 59½, with no exceptions. What is accurate?

options.text: The 10% additional tax can apply, but exceptions exist
The withdrawal is taxed only as a long-term capital gain on the mutual funds held inside the IRA
No 10% additional tax exists on an IRA distribution at any age
The additional tax is waived because his IRA contributions were deductible

explanation: A traditional IRA distribution taken before age 59½ can be subject to a 10% additional tax on top of ordinary income. That tax does not apply to every such distribution: specific exceptions exist, such as disability, certain medical expenses, and other listed cases. The colleague's claim that there are no exceptions is too broad.

distractorExplanations.b: Gives IRA distributions capital-gain treatment. Pre-tax IRA distributions are ordinary income, and the 10% additional tax is a separate issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Denies the 10% additional tax entirely. The tax can apply before 59½ when no exception fits.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses deductibility as a waiver. A deductible contribution does not cancel the additional tax on an early distribution.

prompt: Nelson says he will start required withdrawals from his workplace retirement plan whenever he feels ready to retire. He asks the rep to confirm that the plan has no required beginning date. What should the rep say?

options.text: Required withdrawals start only after he converts the plan balance to a Roth IRA
