He may postpone every required withdrawal until the day he personally feels ready to retire
A required beginning date is an IRA idea and does not apply to his workplace plan

explanation: A workplace retirement plan has a required beginning date for minimum distributions. The tax rules and the plan set that date. It is not the day the participant feels ready to retire. A plan may let someone who is still working delay that date until the person actually separates from service, and that delay is still a required date, not a feeling. Converting the balance to a Roth IRA does not replace it.

distractorExplanations.a: Ties the required beginning date to a Roth conversion. The date is a minimum-distribution rule, not something that starts only if he converts.
distractorExplanations.c: Lets the participant choose the date by personal readiness. The required beginning date is fixed by the rules and the plan, not by how ready he feels.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits required beginning dates to IRAs. A workplace plan has its own required beginning date.

prompt: Ira died at 74, owning two traditional IRAs. His son, age 38, not disabled and not chronically ill, inherited one. Ira's surviving spouse inherited the other. The son must empty his inherited IRA within 10 years. Does that same clock automatically bind the spouse?

options.text: Yes. Both must empty the inherited IRA within 10 years
No. Neither beneficiary has any deadline at all
No. The son is generally on a 10-year clock; the spouse is not automatically
The spouse must empty hers within 10 years, while the son may stretch payments over his full life expectancy as the usual rule

explanation: Many non-spouse designated beneficiaries must empty an inherited IRA by the end of the tenth year after death. Ira's son is 36 years younger, and he is not disabled or chronically ill, so he is not an eligible designated beneficiary. A surviving spouse is an eligible designated beneficiary and is not automatically placed on that same 10-year clock. Other eligible designated beneficiaries exist too, so the 10-year rule is not universal.

distractorExplanations.a: Puts the surviving spouse on the son's 10-year clock. A spouse is an eligible designated beneficiary and is not automatically under that rule.
distractorExplanations.b: Removes the deadline for both of them. The adult son who is not an eligible designated beneficiary generally must empty the IRA within 10 years.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the two rules. The non-spouse son is generally on the 10-year clock; the surviving spouse is the one outside that automatic clock.

prompt: Dana, age 45, opens her first Roth IRA this week by converting pre-tax traditional IRA money. The next day a small earning posts, and she asks whether that earning is already tax-free because the account is a Roth. When is a distribution of Roth IRA earnings qualified?

options.text: The next day, because a Roth label makes every new earning tax-free as soon as it posts
After she has held the Roth for one year, with no other requirement
Only after she moves that earning back into a traditional IRA
After the five-year clock and a qualifying reason, such as age 59½

explanation: Earnings from a Roth IRA are tax-free only as part of a qualified distribution. That requires both the five-year clock, measured from the start of the year of her first Roth IRA, and a qualifying reason such as reaching 59½, death, disability, or a qualified first-home purchase. A conversion this week does not make the next day's earnings tax-free merely because the account is called a Roth.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the Roth label as enough. Earnings are not a qualified distribution the day after a first conversion.
distractorExplanations.b: Shortens the five-year clock to one year and drops the qualifying-reason test. Both the five-year period and a qualifying reason are required.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires a rollover back to a traditional IRA. That move is not what makes Roth earnings a qualified distribution.

prompt: Greta contributed more to her traditional IRA this year than the rules allow for her. She wants to leave the excess invested and ignore it. What has to happen to that excess?

options.text: She has to take the excess out; leaving it invested does not cure it
She may leave it, because the custodian's acceptance of the deposit makes the extra amount an allowed contribution
She should move the excess into a 529, which erases the IRA problem
She should roll the excess into a second IRA, which resets the contribution

explanation: An excess traditional IRA contribution is not cured by leaving it invested. She has to take the excess out of the IRA. When the correction is a withdrawal, the earnings that came from the excess come out with it. Moving the same dollars into a second IRA, or into a 529, does not make the extra amount an allowed contribution.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the custodian's deposit as approval. The custodian's acceptance does not make an excess contribution allowed.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses a 529 transfer as a cure. Taking the excess out of the IRA into a 529 does not, by itself, correct the excess contribution.
distractorExplanations.d: Hides the excess in a second IRA. A rollover between IRAs does not recharacterize an excess as a new allowed contribution.

prompt: Leo's employer deposited a matching contribution into his 401(k). Leo tells the rep the match is his own IRA contribution and should appear in the separate traditional IRA he holds at the brokerage. What is the match?

options.text: His personal IRA contribution, already inside that separate traditional IRA
An employer plan contribution that does not itself go into his separate IRA
A deposit the custodian must sweep from the 401(k) into his traditional IRA on each payday so the match counts as his IRA contribution
A Roth conversion of his IRA, taxed as ordinary income this year

explanation: An employer match is a contribution to the 401(k), not the employee's contribution to his own traditional IRA. It stays in the plan unless a later distributable event lets him roll vested plan money out. The match does not migrate into the separate IRA by itself, and it is not his IRA contribution for the year.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls the match his IRA contribution. The employer deposited it in the 401(k), not in the traditional IRA at the brokerage.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires an automatic sweep into the IRA. A match does not move to his separate IRA, and it does not count as his IRA contribution.
distractorExplanations.d: Misreads the match as a Roth conversion. An employer matching deposit is not a conversion of his IRA.

prompt: Sam rolls over a 401(k) check that mixes his after-tax contributions with pre-tax money. He tells the rep every dollar of the check is tax-free forever because some of it is after-tax basis. What is the right treatment?

options.text: The entire check is tax-free basis and never has to be tracked
The after-tax basis is taxed again, and the pre-tax portion is the tax-free part
After-tax basis must be tracked; the whole check is not automatically tax-free
Basis disappears in a rollover, so every dollar becomes pre-tax and will be taxed a second time when it is later withdrawn

explanation: After-tax contributions are basis that can come back without a second tax, but that basis has to be tracked through the rollover. If the mixed check is rolled into a traditional IRA, later distributions are generally split pro rata between basis and pre-tax money. The basis is not a separate tax-free balance the client can pull out first. Pre-tax money in the same check stays tax-deferred when it is rolled to a traditional IRA. It is not tax-free. Treating the entire check as tax-free erases the difference.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the whole check as basis. Only the after-tax portion is basis, and it still has to be tracked.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the two pieces. After-tax basis is the amount recovered without a second tax; the pre-tax portion is not the tax-free part.
distractorExplanations.d: Says basis vanishes and is taxed twice. Properly tracked after-tax basis is not taxed again, and it does not disappear in the rollover.

prompt: Rita, age 42, takes a hardship withdrawal from her 401(k) for an immediate and heavy financial need. She believes the hardship label by itself removes the 10% additional tax. What is accurate?

options.text: The hardship label removes both ordinary income tax and the 10% additional tax on the withdrawal
A hardship withdrawal is taxed as a long-term capital gain and skips the additional tax
The plan's approval of the hardship waives income tax and the 10% additional tax
The plan's hardship label does not by itself remove the 10% additional tax

explanation: A hardship withdrawal is still a distribution from the plan. It is generally ordinary income. The 10% additional tax can still apply because Rita is under 59½, unless a separate exception in the early-distribution rules fits that distribution. The plan's hardship label does not itself cancel the 10% additional tax.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the hardship label as a full tax waiver. Hardship does not remove ordinary income tax or automatically remove the 10% additional tax.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns capital-gain rates and drops the additional tax. A 401(k) hardship withdrawal is ordinary income, and the 10% tax can still apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the plan's approval to pay the hardship with an IRS waiver. Plan approval does not waive income tax or the 10% additional tax.

prompt: Malik takes a 401(k) loan on the paperwork and repayment schedule his plan requires, and payroll starts the repayments. He asks whether the loan is a taxable distribution the day he receives the money. What is the right answer?

options.text: It is not taxable on day one; a later default can make it a distribution
It is a taxable distribution the day he receives it, even though he repays it exactly on the plan's schedule
It is a Roth conversion and is ordinary income this year
It stays nontaxable even if he stops paying and leaves the employer

explanation: A 401(k) loan that follows the plan's terms is not a taxable distribution on the day Malik receives the money. If he later defaults, or he leaves the employer and does not repay the loan, the unpaid balance can be treated as a taxable distribution. The 10% additional tax can apply to that later distribution if he is under 59½ and no exception fits. Staying on the plan's repayment schedule is what keeps the original loan from being taxed when he receives it.

distractorExplanations.b: Taxes a plan-compliant loan on day one. A loan that follows the plan is not a distribution when it is made.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls the loan a Roth conversion. Borrowing from the 401(k) does not convert pre-tax money to a Roth.
distractorExplanations.d: Says a default stays nontaxable. Stopping repayment can turn the unpaid balance into a taxable distribution.

prompt: A Series 6 rep explains an IRA and recommends that a 401(k) participant roll the plan balance into that IRA. The participant asks whether that explanation makes the rep the plan's ERISA fiduciary. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: Yes. Explaining an IRA makes the rep the plan's ERISA fiduciary
No. That explanation alone does not make the rep the plan's ERISA fiduciary
Yes. Recommending the rollover names the rep as the plan's fiduciary in the plan document
No. The rep also has no duty to support the rollover recommendation

explanation: The plan's ERISA fiduciary is someone with discretionary responsibility for the plan or its assets, or who gives investment advice to the plan for a fee under the ERISA advice test. A Series 6 rep who explains an IRA and recommends a rollover does not become that plan fiduciary merely by the conversation, and the recommendation does not write the rep into the plan document. The rep still needs a reasonable basis to believe the rollover is in the customer's best interest. That duty is separate from being the plan's ERISA fiduciary.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats an IRA explanation as appointment to the plan fiduciary role. Explaining the IRA does not by itself make the rep the plan's ERISA fiduciary.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a rollover recommendation as an appointment written into the plan document. Recommending a rollover does not name the rep as the plan's fiduciary.
distractorExplanations.d: Erases the rep's recommendation duty along with fiduciary status. Not being the plan fiduciary does not mean the rollover recommendation needs no basis.

prompt: A 401(k) participant asks whether to roll the plan balance into an IRA. The rep's only stated reason is that IRAs are more flexible. What does a sound rollover recommendation have to include?

options.text: Nothing beyond the statement that IRAs are more flexible
No comparison, if the participant already prefers an IRA
A comparison of the plan's costs and services with the IRA
A count of the IRA's mutual funds, in place of any look at the plan's costs, services, and features

explanation: A recommendation to roll a workplace plan into an IRA has to compare the plan with the IRA, including costs and services available in each. A slogan that IRAs are more flexible does not make that comparison. Counting mutual funds in the IRA does not replace a look at what the participant would give up in the plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a flexibility slogan as the whole analysis. The recommendation has to compare the plan's costs and services with the IRA.
distractorExplanations.b: Skips the comparison because the participant likes the idea. Preference does not replace a cost-and-service comparison.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a fund count for the comparison. More investment choices do not answer how the plan's costs and services differ from the IRA.

prompt: Noah has a designated Roth account inside his 401(k). He tells the rep to apply every Roth IRA rule to that account because both use the word Roth. What should the rep explain?

options.text: They are the same vehicle, so Roth IRA contribution rules apply unchanged inside the 401(k)
The designated Roth account is his personal traditional IRA held at the employer
It is a 403(b) that any worker may open without an employer
A designated Roth account in the plan, not the same vehicle as a Roth IRA

explanation: A designated Roth account is a separate account inside the 401(k) that holds designated Roth elective deferrals. A Roth IRA is an individual retirement account. Plan deferrals are not Roth IRA contributions, they are not tested under the Roth IRA income limits, and the plan account keeps its own five-year clock. Sharing the word Roth does not make the vehicles the same, so Roth IRA rules do not apply unchanged.

distractorExplanations.a: Merges the two accounts. Roth IRA contribution rules do not govern a designated Roth account inside a 401(k).
distractorExplanations.b: Calls the designated Roth account a traditional IRA. It is a Roth account inside the plan, not a traditional IRA.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigns it to the 403(b) rules and drops the employer. Noah's account is a designated Roth account in his 401(k).

prompt: A client reaches age 59½. A coworker tells the rep that 59½ is the age when required minimum distributions begin. What does age 59½ usually mark?

options.text: The usual age after which the 10% additional tax no longer applies, not an RMD age
The age when required minimum distributions begin from every IRA and workplace plan, with no connection to the 10% additional tax
The age when IRA contributions must stop for good
The age when a Roth conversion of pre-tax money stops being ordinary income

explanation: Age 59½ is the usual age after which the 10% additional tax on early distributions no longer applies. It is not the age at which required minimum distributions begin. Those distributions follow a separate required beginning date, and this item does not state that age. Reaching 59½ also does not stop IRA contributions or make a pre-tax Roth conversion tax-free.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses 59½ as the required-minimum-distribution age and disconnects it from the 10% tax. It is the usual end of that additional tax, not an RMD age.
distractorExplanations.c: Stops contributions at 59½. Earned income can still support an IRA contribution after that birthday.
distractorExplanations.d: Makes a conversion tax-free at 59½. Pre-tax amounts converted to a Roth are still ordinary income in the conversion year.

prompt: Yolanda, age 52, starts substantially equal periodic payments from her IRA so the 10% additional tax does not apply. Two years later she wants to stop the payments and keep that exception. What is the result of stopping early?

options.text: She may stop now and the exception still covers every payment already taken
The payments can avoid the 10% tax, but stopping early can cost that exception
She must stop after two years, and the rep should quote one fixed dollar formula as the only permitted payment
Those payments are available only after age 59½, so they never helped her

explanation: Substantially equal periodic payments can avoid the 10% additional tax before age 59½. Yolanda started at 52, so the series has to continue for the longer of five years or until she reaches 59½. Stopping after two years misses both. The exception can be lost, and the 10% additional tax can be charged back on the payments already taken, with interest. The IRS allows more than one way to set the payment, so there is no single dollar amount to quote, and she is not supposed to stop at year two.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets her stop and keep the exception. Ending the series too soon can cost the exception, including on payments already received.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires her to stop at two years and invents a single dollar formula as the only method. The series is meant to continue, and more than one IRS method can set the payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays the exception until 59½. Substantially equal payments are a way to avoid the 10% tax before that age, if the series is maintained.

prompt: Eli, age 36, wants to use the IRA first-time homebuyer exception for a down payment. He plans to withdraw $10,000 this year and another $10,000 next year, and he calls that his annual housing budget. What limit applies?

options.text: He may withdraw $10,000 for housing every year, with no lifetime cap
The exception covers the full purchase price of a first home
It is a $10,000 lifetime exception, not a yearly housing budget
The first-home exception applies only after age 59½, so a withdrawal at 36 cannot use it

explanation: The IRA first-time homebuyer exception to the 10% additional tax is $10,000 over the individual's lifetime, not $10,000 each year and not the full price of the home. A second $10,000 next year would go beyond that lifetime cap. Pre-tax dollars withdrawn under the exception can still be ordinary income; the exception addresses the additional tax, not income tax.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the lifetime cap into an annual housing allowance. The $10,000 first-home exception does not reset each year.
distractorExplanations.b: Extends the exception to the entire purchase price. The additional-tax exception stops at $10,000 lifetime.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays the first-home exception until 59½. That exception is how a younger owner can avoid the 10% additional tax on up to the lifetime amount, and the cap does not reset each year.

prompt: Nina, age 40, withdraws money from her traditional IRA to pay qualified higher-education expenses. She believes that use removes both the 10% additional tax and ordinary income tax. What is accurate?

options.text: Qualified education costs make the traditional IRA withdrawal free of both ordinary income tax and the 10% additional tax
Education expenses never affect the 10% additional tax on an IRA
The IRA withdrawal is reclassified as a qualified distribution from a 529
The 10% tax can drop away, but the withdrawal can still be ordinary income

explanation: Qualified higher-education expenses can be an exception to the 10% additional tax on an IRA distribution. The exception does not erase income tax. Pre-tax dollars withdrawn from Nina's traditional IRA can still be ordinary income. The withdrawal also stays an IRA distribution; it is not recast as a distribution from a 529 plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Waives ordinary income tax along with the 10% tax. The education exception can remove the additional tax and still leave the withdrawal taxable as income.
distractorExplanations.b: Says education expenses do not affect the 10% tax. Qualified higher-education expenses can be an IRA exception to that additional tax.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves the withdrawal into the 529 rules. Paying tuition from an IRA does not turn the IRA distribution into a 529 distribution.

prompt: The owner of a 529 account withdraws money and spends it on a family vacation. She asks the rep to give that withdrawal the same treatment as money spent on qualified tuition. How should the rep respond?

options.text: Qualified education expenses get the favored treatment; a vacation does not
A family vacation is a qualified education expense and receives the same favored treatment as tuition, fees, and required books
Tuition is a nonqualified expense, just like the vacation
A vacation is qualified, and tuition is not

explanation: Earnings in a 529 withdrawal used for qualified education expenses receive the favored federal treatment and are generally tax-free. A family vacation is not a qualified education expense, so that withdrawal does not get the same treatment. The earnings portion of a nonqualified withdrawal can be included in income and can face an additional tax.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a vacation as a qualified education expense. Travel for a family vacation is not tuition or another qualified education cost.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls tuition nonqualified. Tuition at an eligible institution is a core qualified education expense; the vacation is the nonqualified use.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the two uses. The vacation is not qualified, and qualified tuition is the use that gets the favored treatment.

prompt: A parent owns a 529 account for her daughter. The daughter asks the rep to change the beneficiary to a cousin based on the daughter's signature alone. Who can make that change?

options.text: The daughter, because the beneficiary controls the 529
The owner may name an eligible family member; the child cannot do it alone
No one may change the beneficiary after the account is opened, not even the owner who funded it
Only the college named on the next tuition bill

explanation: The owner of a 529, here the parent, may change the beneficiary to a member of the beneficiary's family. A first cousin is an eligible family member under the 529 rules, so the owner can name that cousin. The daughter cannot make the change on her signature alone, and the college named on a tuition bill does not choose the next beneficiary.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives control to the beneficiary. On a parent-owned 529, the daughter does not change the beneficiary by herself.
distractorExplanations.c: Locks the beneficiary on opening day. The owner can change the beneficiary to an eligible family member.
distractorExplanations.d: Hands the decision to the college. The school receiving tuition does not designate a new 529 beneficiary.

prompt: A city resident hears the treasurer mention a local government investment pool and asks the rep to open that pool as the resident's personal retirement account for old age. What is an LGIP?

options.text: A traditional IRA the city runs for any resident who asks
A Roth IRA that follows government contribution rules
A pool for government funds, not his personal retirement account
The resident's own 457 plan, which the treasurer can retitle into an IRA for that resident's retirement

explanation: A local government investment pool is a vehicle for state and local government cash, offered as a municipal fund security. It is not a traditional IRA, a Roth IRA, or a 457 plan that a resident opens to save for his own retirement. The treasurer's pool cannot be retitled into the resident's personal retirement account.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the pool into a city-run traditional IRA. An LGIP invests government funds; it is not a personal IRA for residents.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls the pool a Roth IRA. Government cash management is not a Roth contribution program for a resident.
distractorExplanations.d: Recasts the LGIP as the resident's 457 plan. A 457 is an employer deferred-compensation plan, and the pool is not one.

prompt: Carl is a W-2 employee whose company does not sponsor a profit-sharing plan. He asks the rep to open a profit-sharing IRA in his brokerage account for this year's pay. How should the rep describe that request?

options.text: A personal IRA he can open at the firm and simply label a profit-sharing IRA
A Roth IRA that accepts only shares of employer stock
A 529 account used to hold an employer's profits for college
An employer plan, not a profit-sharing IRA he opens himself

explanation: A profit-sharing plan is a qualified plan established by an employer, which decides whether to contribute. It is not an IRA the employee opens at a brokerage and labels profit-sharing. Carl's company does not sponsor one, so the rep should not tell him to open a profit-sharing IRA. A Roth IRA limited to employer stock, or a 529, is a different product.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a profit-sharing IRA the client can open alone. Profit sharing is an employer plan, not a label on a personal IRA.
distractorExplanations.b: Substitutes a Roth IRA that holds only employer stock. That is not a profit-sharing plan, and employer stock is not the defining feature.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses a 529 as the profit-sharing vehicle. A 529 is an education account, not an employer profit-sharing plan.

prompt: Rosa participates in her employer's defined-benefit pension. She asks the rep to move her pension into a new mix of mutual funds inside the pension itself. What does that plan provide?

options.text: An individual account balance she and the rep can reallocate among mutual funds inside the pension
A profit-sharing IRA the rep opens and reallocates each year
A benefit set by a formula, not a balance the rep reallocates inside the pension
A self-directed mutual-fund menu inside the pension, so the rep should submit a new fund allocation for her pension balance this week

explanation: A defined-benefit plan promises a benefit calculated from a formula, commonly using compensation and years of service. The participant does not hold a self-directed mutual-fund balance inside that pension for the rep to reallocate. Investing the plan's assets is the plan's job. A separate IRA could hold mutual funds, but that is not a reallocation inside the pension itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives her a participant-directed account inside the pension. A traditional defined-benefit plan promises a formula, not a fund menu she reallocates.
distractorExplanations.b: Renames the pension as a profit-sharing IRA. A defined-benefit plan is not an IRA the rep opens and reallocates.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes a self-directed fund menu inside the pension. The rep does not submit a mutual-fund allocation for a formula pension benefit.

prompt: Jon is still employed and wants an in-service withdrawal from his 401(k). He says every 401(k) must allow that withdrawal on request. Where does the permission come from?

options.text: A federal rule that every 401(k) must allow an in-service withdrawal whenever the participant asks, whatever the plan document says
A ban that no 401(k) may allow an in-service withdrawal, so the document cannot permit one
A required detour that sends the money through a Roth IRA before he can receive it
That plan's document, which may or may not allow an in-service withdrawal

explanation: Whether Jon can take an in-service withdrawal is answered in that plan's document, within the tax limits on the kind of money. Elective deferrals generally stay in the plan while he is employed until age 59½, unless a hardship or another listed exception applies. Other money in the plan can be available in service only when the document allows it. No rule forces every 401(k) to pay on request, and sending the dollars through a Roth IRA does not create a right the document withholds.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes an in-service withdrawal a universal right. The plan document controls, so a request alone does not force every 401(k) to pay one.
distractorExplanations.b: Bans in-service withdrawals in every plan. Some plans allow them when the document and the distribution rules permit.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires a Roth IRA as the path out. An in-service withdrawal, if the plan allows it, is a plan distribution, not a Roth detour.
